sents.vi: Di truyền liên kết hạn chế biến dị tổ hợp, đảm bảo cho sự di truyền bền vững của nhóm tính trạng.

sents.en: Breeders use gene linkage and genetic maps to keep beneficial crop and livestock traits inherited together.
sents.vi: Trong chọn giống, người ta ứng dụng di truyền liên kết và bản đồ gene để các tính trạng tốt luôn di truyền cùng nhau.

sents.en: Chromosome mutations are changes in the structure or number of chromosomes in a cell.
sents.vi: Đột biến NST là những biến đổi về cấu trúc và số lượng NST trong tế bào.

sents.en: Structural chromosome mutations include deletion, duplication, inversion, and translocation.
sents.vi: Đột biến cấu trúc NST gồm các dạng: mất đoạn, lặp đoạn, đảo đoạn và chuyển đoạn.

sents.en: Numerical chromosome mutations include aneuploidy (one or a few pairs) and polyploidy (all chromosome sets).
sents.vi: Đột biến số lượng NST gồm đột biến lệch bội (một hoặc một số cặp) và đột biến đa bội (tất cả các cặp).

sents.en: Polyploid plants have larger vegetative organs, vigorous growth, and often seedless fruits like 3n watermelon.
sents.vi: Thể đa bội ở thực vật có cơ quan sinh dưỡng lớn, sinh trưởng mạnh và thường tạo quả không hạt như dưa hấu 3n.

sents.en: Genetic diseases are functional organ disorders, while genetic defects are morphological abnormalities caused by mutations.
sents.vi: Bệnh di truyền là rối loạn chức năng cơ quan; tật di truyền là bất thường về hình thái do đột biến gây ra.

sents.en: Down syndrome, Turner syndrome, albinism, congenital deaf-mutism, and cleft lip/palate are human genetic conditions.
sents.vi: Hội chứng Down, Turner, bệnh bạch tạng, câm điếc bẩm sinh và tật hở khe môi, hàm là các bệnh, tật di truyền ở người.

sents.en: Marriage within three generations greatly increases the chance of homozygous recessive genetic disorders in children.
sents.vi: Kết hôn gần trong phạm vi ba đời làm tăng mạnh xác suất đồng hợp gene lặn gây bệnh ở con cháu (20–30%).

sents.en: Vietnam’s Marriage and Family Law bans consanguineous marriage within three generations and fetal sex selection.
sents.vi: Luật Hôn nhân và Gia đình nghiêm cấm kết hôn gần trong phạm vi ba đời và lựa chọn giới tính thai nhi.

sents.en: Genetic technology uses plasmid or viral vectors to insert target genes into crops, animals, or microbes.
sents.vi: Công nghệ di truyền dùng plasmid hoặc virus làm thể truyền để cài gene đích vào cây trồng, vật nuôi hoặc vi sinh vật.

sents.en: Genetically modified crops include insect-resistant Bt corn, beta-carotene Golden Rice, and virus-resistant papaya.
sents.vi: Cây trồng biến đổi gene gồm ngô Bt kháng sâu, lúa vàng tổng hợp β-carotene và đu đủ kháng virus.

sents.en: In medicine and forensics, genetic technology produces insulin, enables gene therapy, and matches DNA profiles.
sents.vi: Trong y tế và pháp y, công nghệ di truyền sản xuất insulin, thực hiện liệu pháp gene và đối chiếu dấu vết DNA.

sents.en: Bioethics helps evaluate benefits and risks so genetic technology is applied safely and responsibly.
sents.vi: Đạo đức sinh học giúp đánh giá lợi ích và rủi ro để ứng dụng công nghệ di truyền an toàn, chính đáng.

sents.en: Biological evolution is the change in genetic characteristics of a population over successive generations.
sents.vi: Tiến hóa sinh học là quá trình thay đổi các đặc tính di truyền của quần thể sinh vật qua các thế hệ nối tiếp nhau.

sents.en: Artificial selection keeps and breeds individuals with desired traits to develop improved crops and livestock.
sents.vi: Chọn lọc nhân tạo giữ lại, nhân giống cá thể mang đặc tính tốt và loại thải cá thể kém để tạo giống mới.

sents.en: In natural selection, better-adapted individuals survive and reproduce more, making adaptive traits widespread.
sents.vi: Chọn lọc tự nhiên là quá trình các cá thể thích nghi hơn sống sót và sinh sản nhiều hơn, làm đặc điểm thích nghi phổ biến.

sents.en: Natural selection explains pesticide-resistant insects, antibiotic-resistant bacteria, and new viral strains.
sents.vi: Chọn lọc tự nhiên giải thích sự hình thành côn trùng kháng thuốc trừ sâu, vi khuẩn kháng kháng sinh và chủng virus mới.

sents.en: Lamarck believed organisms actively change under environmental influence and pass acquired traits to offspring.
sents.vi: Lamarck cho rằng sinh vật chủ động biến đổi dưới tác động ngoại cảnh và di truyền các đặc tính thu được cho đời sau.

sents.en: Darwin proposed that undirected individual variations are filtered by natural selection to form adapted species.
sents.vi: Darwin cho rằng biến dị cá thể vô hướng được chọn lọc tự nhiên tích lũy, hình thành loài thích nghi với môi trường.

sents.en: Microevolution is the change in allele and genotype frequencies of a population over generations.
sents.vi: Tiến hóa nhỏ là quá trình biến đổi tần số allele và tần số kiểu gene của quần thể qua các thế hệ.

sents.en: Five evolutionary factors are mutation, gene flow, natural selection, genetic drift, and non-random mating.
sents.vi: Các nhân tố tiến hóa gồm đột biến, di nhập gene, chọn lọc tự nhiên, yếu tố ngẫu nhiên và giao phối không ngẫu nhiên.

sents.en: Life originated on Earth through chemical evolution and prebiotic evolution, followed by biological evolution.
sents.vi: Sự sống trên Trái Đất phát sinh qua tiến hóa hóa học và tiến hóa tiền sinh học, sau đó phát triển qua tiến hóa sinh học.

sents.en: In 1953, Miller and Urey synthesized amino acids from inorganic gases using electric discharges.
sents.vi: Năm 1953, Miller và Urey đã tổng hợp amino acid từ hỗn hợp khí vô cơ nhờ phóng điện.

sents.en: From protocells arose unicellular prokaryotes, then unicellular eukaryotes, and later multicellular organisms.
sents.vi: Từ tế bào sơ khai hình thành sinh vật đơn bào nhân sơ, đơn bào nhân thực rồi sinh vật đa bào.

sents.en: Human evolution progressed through Australopithecus, Homo habilis and Homo erectus, Neanderthals, and modern Homo sapiens.
sents.vi: Quá trình phát sinh loài người trải qua người tối cổ, người cổ đại, người cận đại và người hiện đại (Homo sapiens).

k6l1.title: Introduction to Natural Science
k6l1.text: Natural science studies natural phenomena and their laws. Living things can grow and reproduce, while non-living things cannot. The main branches include biology, chemistry, and physics.

k6l2.title: Laboratory Safety Rules
k6l2.text: Before doing an experiment in the laboratory, always check the warning signs. Wear safety goggles and gloves to protect yourself from toxic or corrosive chemicals. Never eat or drink, and wash your hands with soap afterward.

k6l3.title: How to Use a Magnifying Glass
k6l3.text: A magnifying glass can enlarge small objects from 3 to 20 times. To use it, place the lens close to the specimen and move it slowly away until the image is clear. Clean it with a soft cloth and never look at the Sun.

k6l4.title: Using an Optical Microscope
k6l4.text: An optical microscope magnifies tiny cells from 40 to 3,000 times. First, place the slide on the stage. Look through the eyepiece and turn the coarse knob slowly. Finally, use the fine knob for a clear image.

k6l5.title: Measuring Length Accurately
k6l5.text: The standard unit of length is the meter. Before measuring, estimate the object to select a ruler with a suitable range. Place one end at the zero mark and keep your eyes perpendicular to the scale when reading.

k6l7.title: Measuring Time with a Stopwatch
k6l7.text: The standard unit of time is the second. To time a race or a science experiment, we use a stopwatch. First, press Reset to set the display to zero. Press Start when the event begins, and press Stop at the exact end.

k6l8.title: Measuring Temperature and Thermometers
k6l8.text: Temperature measures how hot or cold an object is. In Vietnam, the common unit is degree Celsius. Liquid thermometers work based on the thermal expansion of liquids. We use a clinical thermometer to check body temperature, and never touch the bulb when reading.

k6l9.title: Diversity and Properties of Substances
k6l9.text: Every object around us is made of one or more substances. Properties like color, state, and boiling point are physical properties. When a substance changes into a new substance, such as iron rusting, it shows a chemical property.

k6l10.title: States of Matter and Changes of State
k6l10.text: Matter commonly exists in three states: solid, liquid, and gas. When heated, ice undergoes melting to become liquid water. Water on Earth turns into vapor by evaporation and forms clouds through condensation.

k6l11.title: Oxygen and Air Environment
k6l11.text: Air around us contains about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen. Oxygen is essential for respiration and burning fuel. To prevent air pollution and acid rain, we should plant more trees and use clean energy.

k6l12.title: Common Materials and Their Properties
k6l12.text: Each material has unique properties suited for specific uses. Metals conduct heat and electricity well, while plastic and wood are poor heat conductors used for pot handles. Rubber is elastic and waterproof for tires. To protect nature, we should reduce, reuse, and recycle household waste.

k6l13.title: Common Raw Materials and Their Uses
k6l13.text: People process natural raw materials such as limestone, ores, and crude oil into useful products. Limestone contains calcium carbonate and is heated to make quicklime and cement. Bauxite ore is processed into aluminum, while iron ore is used to produce cast iron and steel.

k6l14.title: Common Fuels and Energy Security
k6l14.text: Fuels are substances that burn and release a lot of heat. Common fossil fuels include solid coal, liquid gasoline, and natural gas. Because fossil fuels are non-renewable and cause pollution, we must use them safely and develop renewable energy.

k6l15.title: Nutrients in Staple Foods and Foodstuffs
k6l15.text: Daily food gives us energy and nutrients to grow and stay healthy. Carbohydrates in rice and corn are our main energy source. Proteins in meat and beans build the body, while lipids store energy. Fresh vegetables and fruits supply vital minerals and vitamins.

k6l16.title: Pure Substances, Mixtures, and Solubility
k6l16.text: A pure substance contains only one substance, while a mixture contains two or more. When sugar dissolves evenly in water, water is the solvent and sugar water is a homogeneous solution. Unlike solutions, a suspension has solid particles floating in a liquid.

k6l17.title: Methods of Separating Mixtures
k6l17.text: We can separate mixtures using differences in physical properties. Filtration uses filter paper in a funnel to remove insoluble solids from water. To obtain solid salt from seawater, we use evaporation to dryness. A separatory funnel separates two immiscible liquids like cooking oil and water.

k6l18.title: Cells: The Basic Units of Life
k6l18.text: Every living organism is made of tiny cells. A cell carries out life processes like growth, nutrition, respiration, and reproduction. Different cells have different shapes and sizes, and most are so small that we need a microscope to see them.

k6l19.title: Cell Structure and Types of Cells
k6l19.text: All cells have three main components: the cell membrane, cytoplasm, and nucleus or nucleoid. Bacterial cells are prokaryotic because they lack a nuclear membrane. Unlike animal cells, plant cells have a rigid cell wall, a large vacuole, and green chloroplasts for photosynthesis.

k6l20.title: Cell Growth and Cell Division
k6l20.text: Young cells grow into mature cells through metabolism. Once a cell reaches a certain size, it undergoes cell division to form two daughter cells. In multicellular organisms, this process helps the body grow and replaces dead or damaged cells.

k6l21.title: Observing Onion and Fish Egg Cells
k6l21.text: In this lab, we prepare a wet mount of onion epidermal cells on a glass slide. After adding distilled water, we gently lower a coverslip and blot extra water with filter paper. Under the microscope, onion cells show a rigid cell wall, whereas large round fish egg cells do not.

k6l22.title: Living Organisms: Unicellular and Multicellular
k6l22.text: A living organism carries out basic life processes like nutrition, respiration, growth, excretion, and reproduction. A unicellular organism, such as a bacterium or an amoeba, has only one cell. In contrast, a multicellular organism, like a rabbit or a tree, has many specialized cells working together.

k6l23.title: Organization of Multicellular Organisms
k6l23.text: In a multicellular organism, cells are organized from simple to complex levels. Similar cells form a tissue, and different tissues form an organ like the stomach or leaf. Organs cooperate inside an organ system, such as the respiratory system, to keep the whole body alive.

k6l6.title: Measuring Mass with a Balance
k6l6.text: Mass measures the amount of matter in an object, with the kilogram as the base unit. First, estimate the mass and choose a suitable scale. Set the pointer to zero on a dial scale, or press Tare on an electronic balance to subtract the container. Read the value when the scale is steady.

k6l24.title: Observing Unicellular Organisms and Human Organ Systems
k6l24.text: Using a dropper, we place pond water on a slide to observe unicellular organisms like paramecium and green euglena. In the human body, the digestive system absorbs nutrients, while the circulatory system transports oxygen and nutrients throughout the body.

k6l25.title: Classification System and Five Kingdoms
k6l25.text: Biological classification helps scientists identify and study millions of species. The taxonomic ranks go from kingdom down to phylum, class, order, family, genus, and species. All organisms belong to five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, and Animalia.

k6l26.title: Building a Dichotomous Key
k6l26.text: A dichotomous key is the most common classification key in biology. At each step, organisms are divided into two groups based on contrasting traits, such as having legs or not. For example, dragonflies have four wings, while house spiders have eight legs and no wings.

k6l27.title: Structure, Roles, and Prevention of Bacteria
k6l27.text: Bacteria are tiny unicellular prokaryotes with rod, spiral, or spherical shapes. Many use a flagellum to move and pili to attach to host cells. Most bacteria are beneficial, helping decompose waste and make yogurt. Good personal and food hygiene prevents bacterial diseases like cholera and tuberculosis.

k6l28.title: Making Yogurt and Observing Bacteria
k6l28.text: To observe yogurt bacteria, dilute plain yogurt in distilled water and view the slide at 10x and 40x. When making yogurt, cool boiled water to about 50°C before adding condensed milk and starter yogurt. Incubate the jars in a foam box for 10 to 12 hours, then store them in the refrigerator.

k6l29.title: Viruses: Structure, Roles, and Prevention
k6l29.text: A virus has no cell structure and can only replicate inside living host cells. Every virus has a protein coat and a core of DNA or RNA. Viruses cause diseases like flu and dengue fever, and using vaccines is the best way to prevent viral illnesses.

k6l30.title: Protists: Diversity, Roles, and Diseases
k6l30.text: Most protists are microscopic unicellular eukaryotes. An amoeba moves with a pseudopod, while a paramecium uses cilia. Photosynthetic algae produce oxygen and food in water. However, Plasmodium causes malaria via Anopheles mosquitoes, and Entamoeba causes dysentery.

k6l31.title: Lab: Observing Euglena and Paramecium
k6l31.text: Using a dropper, we put 1–2 drops of culture water and a few cotton fibers onto a glass slide, cover with a coverslip, and blot excess water with filter paper. At 40x, green euglena moves with a flagellum while paramecium uses cilia.

k6l32.title: Diversity, Roles, and Safety of Fungi
k6l32.text: Fungi are single- or multi-celled eukaryotes without chlorophyll. In nature, they decompose dead matter into nutrients. People eat mushrooms like shiitake or straw mushroom, use yeast in baking, and use Lingzhi as medicine. However, moldy food and poisonous mushrooms are dangerous, so we keep homes dry and clean.

k6l33.title: Lab: Observing Molds and Mushrooms
k6l33.text: Always wash hands before and after working with mold. Use forceps to place a tiny mold sample on a slide with distilled water, tease it gently, and view at 10x and 40x. For fresh mushrooms like wood ear or straw mushroom, slice lengthwise to identify cap, gills, stalk, and hyphae.

k6l34.title: Plant Diversity, Major Groups, and Roles
k6l34.text: Plants include non-vascular mosses and vascular plants like ferns, gymnosperms, and angiosperms. Mosses live in damp shade and reproduce by spores, while angiosperms have flowers and fruits and the most species. Forests reduce floods and landslides and supply oxygen and food.

k6l35.title: Lab: Observing Moss, Fern, Pine, and Pumpkin
k6l35.text: We examine moss in damp shade using a hand lens and microscope, fern with coiled young fronds and spore clusters, pine with small yellow male cones and larger female cones, and pumpkin with flowers and seeds enclosed inside the fruit.

k6l36.title: Animal Diversity, Groups, and Roles
k6l36.text: Most animals (about 95%) are invertebrates without a backbone, including cnidarians, worms, mollusks, and arthropods with jointed legs. Vertebrates have a backbone and include fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals. Animals support food chains, pollinate plants, and provide food.

k6l37.title: Field Lab: Observing Animals in Nature
k6l37.text: We observe animals in tree canopies, near pond edges, and in water using the naked eye, a hand lens, or binoculars. We note their habitat, traits, and how they move with legs, wings, or fins. Camouflage shapes like a stick insect help animals blend in and survive.

k6l38.title: Biodiversity, Threats, and Conservation
k6l38.text: Biodiversity is clearly shown by species richness in land and water ecosystems. It keeps ecosystems balanced, provides food and raw materials, and protects against disasters. Deforestation and illegal hunting threaten species with extinction, so we must plant forests and protect wildlife.

k6l39.title: Field Study: Exploring Organisms in Nature
k6l39.text: On a field trip, we bring notebooks, a hand lens, binoculars, a butterfly net, an aquatic net, and a label showing species, site, habitat, date, and collector. We use forceps for stinging insects, classify plants and animals using traits and a dichotomous key, and make a photo collection.

k6l40.title: What Is a Force? Push, Pull, and Contact vs. Non-Contact
k6l40.text: A push or pull is a force. A force can change an object’s speed, change its direction of motion, or cause deformation, like stretching a rubber band. A contact force requires touching, whereas a non-contact force acts without touching, like a magnet.

k6l41.title: Force Characteristics and Force Arrows
k6l41.text: Force is measured in newtons (N) using a force meter. Every force has point of application, line, direction, and magnitude. We represent a force by an arrow whose tail sits on the object acted on, direction matches the force, and length fits a chosen scale.

k6l42.title: Spring Deformation and Proportionality to Hanging Mass
k6l42.text: A spring stretches or compresses under force and returns to its original shape when force stops. Extension equals stretched length minus initial length. For a vertical spring, extension is proportional to hanging mass. Exceeding the measuring limit can ruin the spring’s elasticity.

k6l43.title: Gravitational Force, Weight, and Mass
k6l43.text: Any objects with mass attract each other through gravitational force. Weight P is the magnitude of Earth’s pull on an object, measured in newtons, pointing vertically downward. Mass measures amount of matter in kilograms, and weight in N is roughly 10 times mass in kg.

k6l44.title: Friction Forces: Static, Sliding, and Traffic Safety
k6l44.text: Friction is a contact force caused by surface roughness where two objects touch. Static friction holds an object still when pushed, while sliding friction acts when an object slides. Friction can oppose or promote motion. Tire grooves maintain grip to keep road traffic safe.

k6l45.title: Drag Force of Water and Air
k6l45.text: An object moving in water experiences water drag. In Figure 45.1, the force meter reads higher when water is added because it overcomes water drag. Drag increases when area is larger. Sharks and tuna have streamlined shapes to swim easily, and cyclists crouch to cut air drag.

k6l46.title: Energy, Fuels, and Energy Transfer
k6l46.text: Every change in nature needs energy, measured in joules (J). Greater energy can create a stronger force or longer push. Materials like coal, wood, gasoline, and oil that release heat and light when burned are fuels. Energy transfers by force or heat.

k6l47.title: Recognizing and Classifying Forms of Energy
k6l47.text: Moving objects have kinetic energy, while high objects have gravitational potential energy. Chemical energy is stored in food and batteries, and electrical energy runs TVs and computers. Vibrating speakers carry sound energy, and hot stoves release thermal energy.

k6l48.title: Energy Transformation and Conservation
k6l48.text: Energy changes forms and never disappears—this is the law of conservation of energy. A rising ball converts kinetic energy into potential energy. A tennis ball dropped from 1 m bounces lower because part of its energy turns into heat and sound, while total energy stays conserved.

k6l49.title: Useful Energy and Wasted Energy
k6l49.text: When we use energy, part is useful and part is wasted energy, often appearing as heat. Out of 100 J of electricity, an incandescent bulb gives only 5 J of light and 95 J of heat, while an LED lamp gives 80 J of visible light and 20 J of heat.

k6l50.title: Renewable and Non-Renewable Energy Sources
k6l50.text: Natural energy includes renewable and non-renewable sources. Renewable sources like solar, wind, water, biomass, and geothermal energy are replenished quickly and harm the environment less than fossil fuels. Solar panels make electricity, and solar heaters warm water.

k6l51.title: Saving Energy in Daily Life
k6l51.text: Energy saving lowers costs, protects non-renewable resources, and reduces pollution. We save energy by using daylight, turning off unused devices, drying clothes in the sun, and reusing or recycling waste. Using efficient lamps like LED or compact bulbs also cuts power use.

k6l52.title: Apparent Motion of the Sun and Celestial Bodies
k6l52.text: Because Earth rotates from west to east once every 24 hours, the Sun appears to move from east to west. Stars like the Sun emit their own light, while planets orbit stars and moons orbit planets, shining by reflected light. Comets are made of frozen gas and dust.

k6l53.title: The Moon and Its Changing Phases
k6l53.text: The Moon is Earth’s only natural satellite and shines by reflecting sunlight. As the Moon orbits Earth and relative positions change, we see Moon phases from no Moon and crescent to quarter and full Moon. Consecutive full Moons are about four weeks apart.

k6l54.title: The Eight Planets of the Solar System
k6l54.text: The Solar System has the Sun and eight planets orbiting and rotating. Inner planets—Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars—are closer and warmer, while outer planets like Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune are large and cold. Mercury is closest at 0.39 AU, and Neptune is farthest at 30.07 AU.

k6l55.title: The Milky Way and Our Place in the Universe
k6l55.text: The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy of hundreds of billions of celestial bodies with four main spiral arms. Our Solar System is small and sits near the edge of an arm, about 26,000 light-years from the center. Beyond the Milky Way lie trillions of other galaxies studied at observatories.

k7l1.title: Natural Inquiry and Measurement Tools
k7l1.text: In natural inquiry, we propose a problem, make a prediction, plan and carry out a test, and write a report. Key process skills include observation, classification, linking, measurement, and prediction. In Grade 7, a photogate triggers a digital timer to measure time accurately.

k7l2.title: Atomic Structure and the Bohr Model
k7l2.text: Every atom has a tiny nucleus at its center containing positive protons and neutral neutrons. Around the nucleus, negatively charged electrons arrange into shells, with the inner shell holding up to two electrons. Atomic mass is measured in amu.

k7l3.title: Chemical Elements and Symbols
k7l3.text: All atoms with the same number of protons belong to the same chemical element. The proton count equals the atomic number. A chemical symbol uses one or two letters, with the first letter capitalized. For example, sodium has symbol Na and potassium has symbol K.

k7l4.title: Structure of the Periodic Table
k7l4.text: The modern periodic table arranges 118 elements by increasing nuclear charge into periods and groups. Elements in the same horizontal period share the same number of electron shells, while elements in the same group have similar properties. Noble gases sit in group VIIIA.

k7l5.title: Simple Substances, Compounds, and Molecules
k7l5.text: A simple substance contains one element, whereas a compound contains two or more elements. A molecule is a group of bonded atoms that represents a substance. For example, a water molecule has two hydrogens and one oxygen, giving a molecular mass of 18 amu.

k7l6.title: Ionic and Covalent Bonds
k7l6.text: Atoms bond to reach a stable outer shell like noble gases. An ionic bond forms between oppositely charged ions when electrons transfer. A covalent bond forms by sharing electron pairs, as in hydrogen and water.

k7l7.title: Chemical Formulas and Valence
k7l7.text: A chemical formula uses element symbols and subscripts to represent a substance and tell its molecular mass. Valence shows bonding capacity, with hydrogen set at I and oxygen at II. By the valence rule, the product of subscript and valence is equal for both elements in a binary compound.

k7l8.title: Speed and Its Units
k7l8.text: Speed tells how fast or slow something moves and equals distance divided by time, or v = s / t. Common units are m/s and km/h, where 1 m/s equals 3.6 km/h. We can also calculate distance as s = v × t.

k7l9.title: Measuring Speed in the Lab and on the Road
k7l9.text: Measuring speed requires measuring distance and time. In the lab, we mark a start line and a finish line, time three trials with a stopwatch or photogates, and compute v = s / t. On roads, traffic cameras measure vehicle speed to improve safety and prevent accidents.

k7l10.title: Reading and Drawing Distance–Time Graphs
k7l10.text: A distance–time graph plots distance on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis, starting from origin O. A slanted straight line shows motion at steady speed, while a horizontal line parallel to the time axis means the object stops.

k7l11.title: Speed and Road Traffic Safety
k7l11.text: Speeding is a major cause of road accidents. Drivers must follow speed limits and keep a safe distance so they have time to brake. In rain, road grip drops, so maximum speed is lower. The 3-second rule multiplies speed in m/s by three seconds.

k7l12.title: Vibrations, Sound Waves, and Media
k7l12.text: A back-and-forth motion around a balanced point is an oscillation. Every sound source vibrates, and a sound wave spreads that vibration through a medium. Sound travels through solids, liquids, and gases, but it cannot travel in a vacuum.

k7l13.title: Loudness, Amplitude, Pitch, and Frequency
k7l13.text: Vibration amplitude is the distance from equilibrium to the farthest point. A larger sound wave amplitude makes the sound louder. Frequency is oscillations per second, measured in hertz (Hz). Higher frequency produces a higher pitch.

k7l14.title: Sound Reflection and Noise Reduction
k7l14.text: When sound hits a barrier, it bounces back as reflected sound. If it arrives more than 1/15 second after direct sound, we hear an echo. Hard, smooth surfaces reflect sound well, while soft foam reflects sound poorly. Noise barriers and trees help reduce noise pollution.

k7l15.title: Light Energy, Rays, and Shadows
k7l15.text: Light is a form of energy that can power a solar cell or warm water. A light ray is drawn as a straight line with an arrow, modeled by a narrow parallel beam. Behind an obstacle, a narrow light source makes a sharp shadow, whereas a wide source creates a partial shadow too.

k7l16.title: Law of Reflection and Diffuse Reflection
k7l16.text: When light hits a mirror at point I, it forms an incident ray and a reflected ray. The normal is perpendicular to the mirror at I. By the law of reflection, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence. A rough surface causes diffuse reflection in all directions.

k7l17.title: Properties and Construction of Plane Mirror Images
k7l17.text: An image formed by a plane mirror is a virtual image and cannot be caught on a screen. The image size equals the object size, and the distance from the image to the mirror equals the object’s distance. Extending reflected rays with dashed lines locates the virtual image.

k7l18.title: Magnets and Magnetic Poles
k7l18.text: A magnet attracts magnetic materials like iron and steel. When balanced freely, it aligns north and south, showing its North (N) and South (S) poles. Near another magnet, opposite poles attract each other, while like poles repel.

k7l19.title: Magnetic Fields, Field Lines, and Compasses
k7l19.text: A magnetic field surrounds magnets and current-carrying wires. Iron filings form a magnetic spectrum, showing stronger fields where lines are dense. Outside a magnet, field lines run from North to South. A compass uses a magnetic needle to find directions.

k7l20.title: Simple Electromagnets and Their Uses
k7l20.text: Current in a coil creates a magnetic field, and a soft iron core makes it stronger. An electromagnet works only when the switch is closed and current flows. Changing the batteries or reversing poles changes its strength or direction. Scrap cranes and electric bells use electromagnets.

k7l21.title: Overview of Metabolism and Energy Transformation
k7l21.text: Metabolism takes in substances from the environment, transforms them for life, and releases wastes. Energy transformation converts energy from one form to another, such as light to chemical energy. Both processes keep organisms alive and support growth and reproduction.

k7l22.title: Photosynthesis and Leaf Structure
k7l22.text: Photosynthesis occurs mainly in plant leaves inside chloroplasts containing green chlorophyll. Leaves take in water and carbon dioxide to synthesize glucose and release oxygen, converting light energy into chemical energy.

k7l23.title: Factors Influencing Photosynthesis and Tree Protection
k7l23.text: Four main factors affect photosynthesis: light, water, carbon dioxide, and temperature. Most plants photosynthesize best between 25°C and 35°C. If a plant lacks water, its stomata close and CO2 entry drops. Planting and protecting trees keeps air clean and supports life.

k7l24.title: Experiments Proving Starch and Oxygen Production
k7l24.text: To prove photosynthesis makes starch, we cover part of a leaf with black paper, expose it to light, boil it in alcohol to remove chlorophyll, and dip it in iodine. Only the lit part turns blue-purple. In sunlight, aquatic hornwort releases oxygen bubbles that relight a glowing splint.

k7l25.title: Cellular Respiration in Mitochondria
k7l25.text: Cellular respiration takes place inside mitochondria of eukaryotic cells. With the help of oxygen, cells break down glucose into carbon dioxide, water, and usable ATP energy. Synthesis and breakdown of organic matter are opposite yet interdependent.

k7l26.title: Factors Affecting Respiration and Crop Preservation
k7l26.text: Cellular respiration depends on water, oxygen, carbon dioxide, and temperature. Loosening soil gives plant roots more oxygen. To preserve harvested crops, we reduce respiration using dry storage for grains, cold storage for fresh produce, or high-CO2 rooms.

k7l27.title: Experiment on Plant Respiration Using Germinating Seeds
k7l27.text: To observe plant respiration, we soak mung beans in warm water and keep them moist until germination. We place the sprouting seeds and a beaker of clear limewater under Bell Jar A. After one hour, carbon dioxide released by respiration forms a white precipitate on the limewater in Jar A, while control Jar B stays clear.

k7l28.title: Gas Exchange in Plants and Animals
k7l28.text: Gas exchange occurs by diffusion. Plants exchange gases through leaf stomata, taking in CO2 during photosynthesis and O2 during respiration. Animals use skin, tracheal systems, gills, or lungs. In humans, air passes through the airway to lung alveoli.

k7l29.title: Water Polarity and Nutrient Roles
k7l29.text: Because a water molecule is polar, water dissolves many substances and transports nutrients inside organisms. Water makes up about 70% of human body mass and helps regulate temperature. Plants absorb mineral nutrients like nitrogen from soil, while animals need proteins, carbohydrates, lipids, vitamins, and minerals.

k7l30.title: Water Absorption, Transport, and Transpiration in Plants
k7l30.text: Root hair cells absorb water and minerals from soil, which travel upward to leaves through xylem. Leaves send organic food to other organs through phloem. Leaf transpiration pulls water upward, cools the leaf, and opens stomata for gas exchange.

k7l31.title: Digestion, Water Balance, and Blood Circulation in Animals
k7l31.text: Food is broken down into simple nutrients in the digestive tract and absorbed into the blood. Water enters through food and drink and leaves via urine and sweat. In humans, pulmonary circulation carries blood to the lungs, while systemic circulation delivers oxygen and nutrients to body organs.

k7l32.title: Experiments on Stem Transport and Leaf Transpiration
k7l32.text: When celery stalks stand in colored water, dye travels upward through xylem bundles and tints the leaves. In the second experiment, a clear plastic bag covers leafy Pot B and leafless Pot A. After 30 minutes, water droplets appear inside Pot B’s bag, proving leaves transpire water.

k7l33.title: Responsiveness in Organisms and Animal Behavior
k7l33.text: Responsiveness is how living organisms react to environmental stimuli, helping them survive and grow. In animals, behavior is a chain of responses to internal or external stimuli. Innate behavior is present from birth, while learned behavior develops through experience.

k7l34.title: Practical Applications of Responsiveness and Behavior
k7l34.text: In farming, trellises help climbing crops grow using touch responsiveness, while light traps catch crop pests. In livestock care, clapping calls fish to feed and trained dogs herd sheep. In daily life, good study and health habits grow through steady repetition.

k7l35.title: Experiments on Hydrotropism and Phototropism
k7l35.text: When a small porous water pot is placed on one side of a planter, seedling roots grow toward the moisture, proving hydrotropism. Under a cardboard box with a side hole, bean stems bend toward the incoming light, demonstrating phototropism.

k7l36.title: Growth, Development, and Plant Meristems
k7l36.text: Growth is the increase in body size and mass, while development includes growth, cell differentiation, and organ formation. In plants, meristems are dividing cells that drive growth: apical meristems increase length at root tips and buds, whereas lateral meristems increase thickness.

k7l37.title: Factors and Applications of Growth and Development
k7l37.text: Growth and development depend on temperature, light, water, nutrients, and hormones. Sunlight helps animals make vitamin D for strong bones. Farmers use growth stimulators for fruit and fiber crops, inhibitors to stop garlic sprouting, and eliminate stagnant water to kill mosquito larvae.

k7l38.title: Observing Plant and Animal Growth and Development
k7l38.text: In this lab, we soak healthy bean seeds in warm water, plant them in bright light, and measure stem height and leaf count daily. Comparing animal life cycles shows that a butterfly changes form through egg, larva, pupa, and adult, whereas a chick hatches resembling the adult.

k7l39.title: Asexual Reproduction and Plant Propagation
k7l39.text: Asexual reproduction forms offspring from one parent without gamete fusion, keeping parental traits. Plants use vegetative organs like roots, stems, or leaves, while animals use budding, fragmentation, or parthenogenesis. Farmers apply stem cutting, layering, grafting, and tissue culture.

k7l40.title: Sexual Reproduction in Plants and Animals
k7l40.text: Sexual reproduction unites male and female gametes to form a zygote. In flowering plants, pollination brings pollen to the stigma, followed by fertilization so ovules become seeds and the ovary becomes a fruit. In animals, fertilization may be external or internal, with egg-laying or live-bearing species.

k7l41.title: Factors and Control of Reproduction in Organisms
k7l41.text: Reproduction is influenced by genetics, hormones, age, light, and temperature. Farmers light dragon fruit plants at night for off-season flowering and protect pollinating insects. In livestock farming, artificial insemination and embryo transfer increase offspring numbers.

k7l42.title: The Living Organism as a Unified Whole
k7l42.text: Every living organism is a unified whole. The body absorbs nutrients, water, minerals, and oxygen from the environment so cells can grow, divide, and respond, releasing carbon dioxide and wastes. Metabolism, growth, development, responsiveness, and reproduction work together closely.

k8l30.title: Overview of Human Body Regions and Organ Systems
k8l30.text: The human body has head, neck, trunk, arms, and legs. Its organ systems include musculoskeletal, circulatory, respiratory, digestive, excretory, nervous and sense organs, endocrine, and reproductive. Each system has a distinct role and links closely with others.

k8l31.title: The Musculoskeletal System, Bone Health, and Fracture First Aid
k8l31.text: The human musculoskeletal system includes bones, joints, and muscles. Minerals give bones firmness while organic matter gives flexibility. Poor posture or heavy uneven loads can cause spinal curvature, and low calcium/phosphorus can lead to osteoporosis. Splints and bandages immobilize a fracture during first aid.

k8l32.title: Nutrition, Digestion, Digestive Diseases, and Food Safety
k8l32.text: Nutrition uses food nutrients—carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, and minerals—to build the body and supply energy. Digestion breaks food down along the digestive tract, mostly in the small intestine, while the large intestine reabsorbs water. Safe food handling and balanced meals prevent ulcers and food poisoning.

k8l33.title: Blood Components, Immunity, Blood Groups, and Circulation
k8l33.text: Blood contains plasma plus red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. B cells make antibodies against antigens, and vaccines build immunity. The heart and blood vessels pump blood through pulmonary and systemic circuits.

k8l34.title: Human Respiratory System, Smoking Harm, and Rescue
k8l34.text: The respiratory system has airways and lungs where alveoli exchange gases by diffusion. Inhalation expands chest volume so air enters. Tobacco smoke has CO, NOx, and nicotine that damage airways and lungs. Mouth-to-mouth and chest compression are used in resuscitation.

k8l35.title: Excretory System, Kidney Diseases, and Dialysis/Transplant
k8l35.text: The excretory system removes wastes, with kidneys excreting up to 90% of wastes via urine. Each kidney has about one million functional units. High salt levels can form kidney stones, and dialysis or a kidney transplant helps patients with kidney failure.

k8l36.title: Internal Environment, Homeostasis, and Blood Tests
k8l36.text: The internal environment includes blood, tissue fluid, and lymph. Keeping it balanced lets cells and organs work normally. High glucose over time can indicate diabetes, and prolonged high uric acid risks gout or kidney trouble. Blood tests help check these levels.

k8l37.title: Nervous System, Vision, and Hearing in Humans
k8l37.text: The nervous system has central (brain, spinal cord) and peripheral (nerves, ganglia) parts. Addictive substances like nicotine and narcotics harm nervous function. Vision focuses light on the retina via cornea and lens, while hearing transmits vibrations through outer, middle, and inner ear to the brain.

k8l38.title: Human Endocrine Glands, Blood Sugar, and Goiter
k8l38.text: Endocrine glands release hormones into blood to regulate organs. The pancreas secretes insulin to lower blood sugar and glucagon to raise it. Lack of insulin or its effect causes diabetes, while lack of iodine can lead to goiter.

k8l39.title: Skin Structure, Body Temperature, and Thermoregulation
k8l39.text: Human skin has epidermis, dermis, and fat layers, protecting the body and aiding thermoregulation. Normal body temperature is about 37°C. When it is hot, capillaries dilate and sweating rises to release heat; when very cold, heat loss drops and shivering helps generate warmth.

k8l40.title: Human Reproduction, Menstrual Cycle, and Reproductive Health
k8l40.text: In humans, fertilization unites sperm and egg in the fallopian tube, and implantation occurs when the embryo attaches in the uterus. Without fertilization, the uterine lining sheds in menstruation. Healthy habits and prevention protect against unintended pregnancy and diseases.

k8l41.title: Living Environments, Ecological Factors, and Tolerance Limits
k8l41.text: Organisms live in four main habitats: terrestrial, aquatic, soil, and living hosts. Ecological factors include non-living abiotic factors like light and temperature, and living biotic factors including humans. Each species survives within its ecological tolerance range.

k8l42.title: Populations and Their Key Characteristics
k8l42.text: A population consists of individuals of the same species living together and reproducing. Its main features are population size, density, sex ratio, age groups, and distribution (uniform, clumped, or random). Protecting habitats like national parks helps populations survive.

k8l43.title: Biological Communities and Biodiversity Protection
k8l43.text: A biological community brings together populations of different species in one habitat. Communities differ in diversity and species composition, including dominant species and characteristic species. Conservation laws, reserves, and preventing fires protect biodiversity.

k8l44.title: Ecosystem Structure, Food Webs, and Energy Flow
k8l44.text: An ecosystem combines a biological community with its non-living environment. Living organisms include producers, consumers, and decomposers. Feeding links form food chains and food webs, while solar energy flows one way through trophic levels and returns as heat.

k8l45.title: The Biosphere and Major Biomes on Earth
k8l45.text: The biosphere encompasses all life on Earth and its non-living surroundings across lithosphere, atmosphere, and hydrosphere. Regional climates create biomes on land, in freshwater lakes and rivers, and in the ocean from surface plankton to deep-sea benthos.

k8l46.title: Natural Balance, Biological Control, and Ecosystem Stability
k8l46.text: Natural balance maintains dynamic stability across populations, communities, and ecosystems. Populations self-regulate around carrying capacity, while biological control links predators and prey like lynx and hares. Preventing pollution, overexploitation, and invasive species protects equilibrium.

k8l47.title: Environmental Protection, Pollution Control, and Climate Adaptation
k8l47.text: Environmental pollution comes from industrial emissions, misused pesticides, radioactive waste, and untreated sewage. Treating waste, using renewable energy, and sorting household trash reduce harm. Building dikes, planting mangroves, and protecting endangered wildlife sustain our planet.

k9l36.title: Introduction to Genetics and Mendel’s Terms
k9l36.text: Heredity passes traits to offspring, while variation shows differences from parents. Mendel studied pea plants and proposed hereditary factors, now called genes, which make up the core of genetics. A recessive trait appears when homozygous recessive.

k9l37.title: Mendel’s Laws of Segregation and Independent Assortment
k9l37.text: Mendel’s law of segregation shows allele pairs separate into gametes, giving a 3:1 ratio in F2. A test cross checks an unknown dominant genotype using a recessive partner. Under independent assortment, two gene pairs produce four gamete types and a 9:3:3:1 ratio in F2.

k9l38.title: Nucleic Acids, DNA Structure, Genes, and RNA
k9l38.text: Nucleic acids include DNA and RNA. DNA forms a double helix with complementary base pairing of A with T and G with C, storing and transmitting genetic information. A gene is a functional DNA segment. Single-stranded RNA uses A, U, G, and C in mRNA, tRNA, and rRNA.

k9l39.title: DNA Replication and Transcription to RNA
k9l39.text: Before cell division, DNA replication unwinds strands and pairs A with T and G with C to make two identical copies, ensuring genetic continuity. In transcription, RNA is synthesized from a gene template with A pairing with U instead of T. PCR copies DNA in the lab.

k9l40.title: Genetic Code, Translation, and Gene-to-Trait Relationship
k9l40.text: The genetic code uses three-base codons on mRNA, with 64 codons in total. Translation builds a polypeptide from mRNA using tRNAs and ribosomes. Information flows from gene to mRNA to protein and trait, shaped by genomes and environment.

k9l41.title: Gene Mutations, Causes, Effects, and Applications
k9l41.text: A gene mutation changes gene structure, sometimes at a single pair as a point mutation. Mutations may be beneficial, harmful, or neutral depending on environment. Radiation and chemicals can raise mutation rates, while selective breeding uses useful mutations like salt-tolerant rice.

k9l42.title: Chromosomes, Diploid vs. Haploid Sets, and Microscopy
k9l42.text: Chromosomes in the nucleus package long DNA with histone proteins and carry genes in linear order. Body cells have a diploid (2n) set of homologous pairs, while gametes have a haploid (n) set. Chromosomes are clearest at metaphase under the microscope.

k9l43.title: Mitosis, Meiosis, and Fertilization
k9l43.text: Mitosis divides one cell into two with the same chromosome set for growth and repair. Meiosis divides twice in gamete-forming cells to make four cells with half the chromosomes. Together with fertilization, they keep species chromosome counts steady and create recombination variation.

k9l44.title: Sex Chromosomes, Sex Determination, and Sex Differentiation
k9l44.text: Human somatic cells have 44 autosomes plus XX in females or XY in males. Sex determination comes from chromosome segregation in gamete formation and fertilization, giving roughly a 1:1 ratio. Hormones and temperature also influence sex differentiation.

k9l45.title: Linked Inheritance and Breeding Applications
k9l45.text: Thomas Hunt Morgan discovered linked inheritance in fruit flies in 1910. When genes lie on the same chromosome, they tend to pass together during meiosis, limiting recombination and giving a 1:1 test-cross ratio. Breeders use gene linkage to keep desirable traits together.

k9l46.title: Chromosomal Mutations: Structural and Numerical
k9l46.text: Chromosome mutations alter chromosome structure or number. Structural types include deletion, duplication, inversion, and translocation. Numerical types include aneuploidy, such as trisomy 21 Down syndrome, and polyploidy, which produces large, seedless 3n fruits in plants.

k9l47.title: Human Genetics, Genetic Disorders, and Family Planning
k9l47.text: Human genetic diseases and defects arise from gene or chromosome mutations, worsened by radiation and toxic chemicals. Consanguineous marriage within three generations raises recessive disorder risk, so the law bans close-kin marriage and fetal sex selection.

k9l48.title: Applications of Genetic Technology and Bioethics
k9l48.text: Genetic technology uses a plasmid vector to create transgenic crops like Bt corn and Golden Rice. In medicine, it produces insulin and enables gene therapy, while DNA profiling aids forensics and biosafety. Bioethics guides safe, responsible use.

k9l49.title: Evolution, Artificial Selection, and Natural Selection
k9l49.text: Biological evolution changes a population’s genetic traits over generations. In artificial selection, humans breed wild mustard into cabbage or broccoli and select fast-growing chickens. In natural selection, better-adapted individuals like dark moths on sooty bark survive and reproduce more.

k9l50.title: Evolutionary Theories and Mechanisms
k9l50.text: Lamarck proposed inheritance of acquired traits, while Darwin explained adaptation through individual variation and natural selection. The modern synthesis defines microevolution as changes in population allele frequencies driven by mutation, gene flow, natural selection, genetic drift, and non-random mating.

k9l51.title: Origin of Life, Diversification of Organisms, and Human Evolution
k9l51.text: Life began on early Earth through chemical evolution and prebiotic evolution forming protocells with self-replicating nucleic acids. Unicellular prokaryotes gave rise to eukaryotes and multicellular organisms. Human evolution led through early hominins to modern Homo sapiens.

k6l4.q: Which part of the microscope do you look into with your eye?

a.quiz: Eyepiece

k6l4.expl: The eyepiece is the top lens that you look through to observe the specimen.

k6l4.q: Which knob should you turn slowly at the final step to make the image sharp and clear?

a.quiz: Fine adjustment knob

k6l4.hint: Use the smaller focusing knob at the end.
k6l4.expl: Turning the fine adjustment knob slowly brings the specimen into sharp focus.

k6l4.q: How should you carry an optical microscope safely?
opts: Hold it by the eyepiece only
Hold the arm with one hand and support the base with the other
Carry it upside down by the stage
Drag it across the table with wet hands

a.quiz: Hold the arm with one hand and support the base with the other

k6l4.expl: Always hold the arm with one hand and support the base with the other hand when moving a microscope.

k6l4.q: Place the glass ___ on the stage and secure it with stage clips.

a.quiz: slide

k6l4.sentence: Place the glass slide on the stage.
k6l4.expl: The prepared slide containing the specimen is placed on the stage.

k6l4.q: Clean the eyepiece and objective lenses with special ___ before and after use.

a.quiz: lens paper

k6l4.expl: Always wipe lenses with special lens paper to prevent scratches and moisture damage.

k6l4.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k6l4.raw: An optical microscope can magnify an object from 40 to 3,000 times.
k6l4.sentence: An optical microscope can magnify an object from 40 to 3,000 times.
k6l4.expl: Optical microscopes have a magnification range of 40x to 3,000x.

k6l4.hint: Three items are parts of an optical microscope.
k6l4.expl: A leaf vein is a plant specimen, not a part of a microscope.

k6l4.q: When lowering the objective lens, be careful not to let it touch the glass slide.
k6l4.hint: Think about protecting the lens and slide.
k6l4.expl: Letting the objective lens hit the slide can crack the glass and scratch the lens.

k6l4.q: Find and correct the mistake: Touch the microscope lenses with wet or dirty hands.

a.fix: Never touch the microscope with wet or dirty hands.

k6l4.raw: Never touch the microscope with wet or dirty hands.
k6l4.hint: Should hands be wet or dry?
k6l4.expl: Keep hands clean and dry; clean lenses only with special lens paper.

k6l5.q: What is the standard unit of length in Vietnam and the SI system?

a.quiz: Meter (m)

k6l5.expl: The meter (m) is the official base unit of length in Vietnam and the International System of Units (SI).

k6l5.q: What does the "measuring range" (GHĐ) of a ruler mean?
opts: The distance between two adjacent marks
The maximum length printed on the ruler
The zero mark on the ruler

a.quiz: The maximum length printed on the ruler

k6l5.hint: Think about the largest value a ruler can measure in one go.
k6l5.expl: The measuring range (GHĐ) is the maximum length marked on the measuring instrument.

k6l5.q: Which measuring tool is best for measuring the circumference of a cup opening?

a.quiz: A flexible measuring tape

k6l5.expl: A flexible measuring tape easily wraps around curved surfaces like a cup opening.

k6l5.q: How should you position your eyes when reading a measurement on a ruler?
opts: Perpendicular (at 90 degrees) to the ruler edge

a.quiz: Perpendicular (at 90 degrees) to the ruler edge

k6l5.hint: Avoid parallax error by looking straight down.
k6l5.expl: Your eyes must look perpendicular to the ruler edge at the other end of the object to read accurately.

k6l5.q: How many centimeters are equal to 1 meter?

a.quiz: 100 cm

k6l5.q: The ___ of a ruler is the length between two consecutive scale marks.

a.quiz: smallest division

k6l5.sentence: The smallest division is the length between two consecutive marks.
k6l5.hint: Think about the finest unit a ruler can show.
k6l5.expl: The smallest division (ĐCNN) is the distance between two adjacent lines on a ruler.

k6l5.q: Always ___ the length before measuring so you can choose a suitable ruler.

a.quiz: estimate

k6l5.hint: Make a quick guess of the size first.
k6l5.expl: Estimating the length beforehand helps select a ruler with an appropriate measuring range and smallest division.

k6l5.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k6l5.raw: Align one end of the object with the zero mark on the ruler.
k6l5.sentence: Align one end of the object with the zero mark on the ruler.
k6l5.expl: Proper alignment at the zero mark ensures an accurate length measurement.
A magnifying glass is used to enlarge small objects, not to measure length.

k6l5.q: One kilometer is equal to 1,000 meters.
k6l5.expl: 1 km = 1,000 m, commonly used for long distances like between Hanoi and Hue.

k6l5.q: Find and correct the mistake: Look at the ruler from a slanted angle when reading the measurement.

a.fix: Look perpendicular to the ruler when reading the measurement.

k6l5.raw: Look perpendicular to the ruler when reading the measurement.
k6l5.expl: Looking at a slanted angle causes parallax error; always look perpendicular to the scale.

k6l7.q: What is the standard base unit of time in Vietnam and the SI system?

a.quiz: Second (s)

k6l7.expl: In Vietnam’s legal measurement system and the SI system, the base unit of time is the second (s).

k6l7.q: Which type of clock is best for timing sports races and laboratory experiments?

a.quiz: Stopwatch

k6l7.hint: It has Start, Stop, and Reset buttons.
k6l7.expl: A stopwatch measures short time intervals with high precision for sports and experiments.

k6l7.q: What should you press on a digital stopwatch BEFORE starting a new measurement?

a.quiz: Reset

k6l7.expl: Pressing Reset sets the stopwatch back to zero so the measurement starts accurately.

k6l7.q: How does a sundial measure time?
opts: By the shadow cast under sunlight

a.quiz: By the shadow cast under sunlight

k6l7.expl: A sundial tells time using the shadow of a pointer cast by sunlight onto a marked dial.

k6l7.q: How many seconds are equal to 2 minutes?
k6l7.expl: Since 1 minute equals 60 seconds, 2 minutes equal 2 × 60 = 120 seconds.

k6l7.q: In the SI system, the base unit of time is the ___, symbolized by s.

a.quiz: second

k6l7.sentence: The base unit of time is the second.
k6l7.hint: Think of the smallest common unit on a stopwatch.
k6l7.expl: The second (s) is the standard base unit of time.

k6l7.q: Before timing an experiment, press ___ to set the stopwatch back to zero.

a.quiz: Reset

k6l7.hint: Make sure the screen reads 0:0000 before starting.
k6l7.expl: Pressing Reset clears previous readings and sets the stopwatch to zero.

k6l7.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k6l7.raw: Press Reset to return the stopwatch to zero before starting.
k6l7.sentence: Press Reset to return the stopwatch to zero before starting.
k6l7.expl: Always zero the stopwatch before measuring.
A vernier caliper measures length/diameter, not time.

k6l7.q: Estimating time beforehand helps us choose a suitable clock with an appropriate measuring range.
k6l7.hint: Think about why estimation is important before measuring.
k6l7.expl: Estimating the duration first helps select the right type of clock or stopwatch.

k6l7.q: Find and correct the mistake: Start timing with a stopwatch without resetting it to zero first.

a.fix: Press Reset to set the stopwatch to zero before starting.

k6l7.raw: Press Reset to set the stopwatch to zero before starting.
k6l7.hint: What must the stopwatch show before you press Start?
k6l7.expl: Forgetting to reset causes an incorrect reading; always reset to zero first.

opts: How hot or cold an object is

a.quiz: How hot or cold an object is

k6l8.hint: Think about hot and cold sensations.
k6l8.expl: Temperature is the physical quantity that measures the degree of hotness or coldness of an object.

k6l8.q: On the Celsius scale, what are the temperatures of melting ice and boiling water?

a.quiz: 0°C and 100°C

k6l8.hint: Anders Celsius divided this interval into 100 equal parts.
k6l8.expl: In the Celsius scale, melting ice is defined as 0°C and boiling water is 100°C.

k6l8.q: Which physical phenomenon is used as the working principle of liquid thermometers?

a.quiz: Thermal expansion of liquids

k6l8.hint: Liquids expand when heated and rise in the tube.
k6l8.expl: Liquids expand when heated and contract when cooled, allowing temperature measurement.

k6l8.q: What is normal human body temperature on the Celsius scale?
k6l8.expl: Normal healthy human body temperature is approximately 37°C.

k6l8.q: Which action is INCORRECT when using a mercury clinical thermometer?
opts: Cleaning the thermometer with medical cotton before use
Shaking the thermometer down before measuring
Holding the thermometer bulb tightly while reading the temperature
Reporting immediately to the teacher if the thermometer breaks

a.quiz: Holding the thermometer bulb tightly while reading the temperature

k6l8.hint: Your hand warmth can change the reading.
k6l8.expl: Holding the bulb transfers body heat from your hand, causing an inaccurate reading.

k6l8.q: In Vietnam, the common unit of temperature is degree ___, symbolized by °C.

a.quiz: Celsius

k6l8.sentence: The common unit of temperature is degree Celsius.
k6l8.hint: Named after Swedish scientist Anders Celsius.
k6l8.expl: Degree Celsius (°C) is the standard temperature unit used in Vietnam.

k6l8.q: Liquids ___ when heated, which is the principle behind liquid thermometers.

a.quiz: expand

k6l8.hint: The liquid level rises inside the glass tube when warmed.
k6l8.expl: Thermal expansion causes liquids to occupy more volume as temperature rises.

k6l8.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k6l8.raw: Temperature is the measure of how hot or cold an object is.
k6l8.sentence: Temperature is the measure of how hot or cold an object is.

k6l8.hint: Three items are types of thermometers.
k6l8.expl: A stopwatch measures time, not temperature.

k6l8.q: Mercury inside a broken clinical thermometer is toxic, so you must not touch it with bare hands.
k6l8.hint: Think about laboratory safety with mercury.
k6l8.expl: Mercury is a poisonous liquid metal that evaporates easily; report broken thermometers immediately.

k6l8.q: Find and correct the mistake: Hold the thermometer bulb tightly with your fingers while reading the temperature.

a.fix: Avoid holding the thermometer bulb while reading the temperature.

k6l8.raw: Avoid holding the thermometer bulb while reading the temperature.
k6l8.hint: Where should you hold the thermometer?
k6l8.expl: Hold the stem of the thermometer rather than the bulb so hand heat does not alter the reading.

k6l9.q: Which of the following is an artificial object made by humans?

a.quiz: Long Bien Bridge

k6l9.hint: Think about something built by people.
k6l9.expl: Long Bien Bridge is built by humans, so it is an artificial object.

k6l9.q: Which group lists ONLY physical properties of a substance?
opts: Color, state, smell, and melting point

a.quiz: Color, state, smell, and melting point

k6l9.hint: Physical properties do not create a new substance.
k6l9.expl: State (solid, liquid, gas), color, smell, and melting point are physical properties.

k6l9.q: What defines a chemical property of a substance?
opts: Its ability to dissolve in water
Its transformation into a new substance

a.quiz: Its transformation into a new substance

k6l9.hint: Look for the creation of a new substance.
k6l9.expl: A chemical property is shown when a substance transforms into one or more new substances.

k6l9.q: Which statement describes a chemical property of iron?
opts: An iron nail is hard and gray
An iron nail is attracted by a magnet
An iron nail forms brown, brittle rust in moist air
An iron nail is a solid at room temperature

a.quiz: An iron nail forms brown, brittle rust in moist air

k6l9.expl: Iron reacting with air and moisture to form brown rust is a chemical change showing its chemical property.

k6l9.q: In the experiment heating salt and sugar, which substance changed into a new substance?

a.quiz: Sugar only

k6l9.hint: Sugar turned dark brown and produced smoke.
k6l9.expl: When heated, sugar decomposed into a dark brown substance with smoke, demonstrating a chemical property.

k6l9.q: Distilled water is an object made of a single ___, which is water.

a.quiz: substance

k6l9.sentence: Distilled water is made of a single substance.
k6l9.expl: Every object is composed of one or more substances; distilled water consists of pure water.

k6l9.q: Color, taste, melting point, and boiling point are ___ properties of a substance.

a.quiz: physical

k6l9.hint: These properties can be observed without forming a new substance.
k6l9.expl: Physical properties describe characteristics that do not involve changing into a new substance.

k6l9.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k6l9.raw: Objects around us are made of one or more substances.
k6l9.sentence: Objects around us are made of one or more substances.
k6l9.expl: Where there is an object, there is substance.
Rusting in air forms a new substance (chemical property), whereas color, smell, and boiling point are physical properties.

k6l9.q: Burning coal to produce carbon dioxide gas is an example of a chemical property.
k6l9.hint: Does burning coal create a new substance?
k6l9.expl: Coal reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide, a new substance, which is a chemical property.

k6l9.q: Find and correct the mistake: Melting ice into liquid water creates a brand-new chemical substance.

a.fix: Melting ice into liquid water is a physical property (change of state), not a new substance.

k6l9.raw: Melting ice into liquid water is a physical property (change of state), not a new substance.
k6l9.hint: Is ice still water after it melts?
k6l9.expl: Ice and liquid water are the same substance in different physical states (solid and liquid).

k6l10.q: Which state of matter has a fixed shape and cannot flow?

a.quiz: Solid

k6l10.hint: Think about wood, iron, or ice.
k6l10.expl: Solids have particles arranged in a fixed order, giving them a fixed shape and preventing flow.

k6l10.q: Why can you smell perfume across a room shortly after opening the bottle?
opts: Gas particles spread easily in all directions

a.quiz: Gas particles spread easily in all directions

k6l10.hint: Think about the spreading ability of gases.
k6l10.expl: Perfume vapor is in the gas state, where particles move freely and spread in all directions.

k6l10.q: What is the process of a liquid changing into a solid called?

a.quiz: Freezing

k6l10.hint: Think about water turning into ice in winter.
k6l10.expl: Freezing (solidification) is the process in which a substance changes from a liquid to a solid.

k6l10.q: How does evaporation differ from boiling?
opts: Evaporation occurs at any temperature, while boiling occurs only at the boiling point

a.quiz: Evaporation occurs at any temperature, while boiling occurs only at the boiling point

k6l10.hint: Compare the temperatures at which each process happens.
k6l10.expl: Evaporation takes place on the liquid surface at any temperature, whereas boiling occurs at a fixed boiling point.

k6l10.q: Which process turns water vapor in the atmosphere into tiny liquid droplets forming clouds?

a.quiz: Condensation

k6l10.hint: Warm water vapor rises and cools down in the sky.
k6l10.expl: Condensation is the change of state from gas (water vapor) to liquid droplets, forming clouds.

k6l10.q: Air inside a syringe is in the ___ state and can be compressed easily.

a.quiz: gas

k6l10.sentence: Air in a syringe is easy to compress.
k6l10.hint: Remember the syringe experiment with air.
k6l10.expl: Gases have wide spaces between particles, making them easy to compress.

k6l10.q: Water melts and freezes at the same temperature of ___.
k6l10.hint: Think of the freezing point of pure water.
k6l10.expl: Every pure substance melts and freezes at the same temperature; for water, it is 0°C.

k6l10.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k6l10.raw: Solids have a fixed shape and are very difficult to compress.
k6l10.sentence: Solids have a fixed shape and are very difficult to compress.
k6l10.expl: This describes the main properties of solids.

k6l10.hint: Three items are processes of state change.
k6l10.expl: Thermometer is a measuring instrument, not a change of state.

k6l10.q: Condensation and evaporation can occur at any temperature.
k6l10.expl: Both evaporation and condensation happen across a wide range of temperatures, unlike boiling.

k6l10.q: Find and correct the mistake: Boiling happens only on the surface of a liquid at any temperature.

a.fix: Boiling happens both on the surface and inside a liquid at its boiling point.

k6l10.raw: Boiling happens both on the surface and inside a liquid at its boiling point.
k6l10.hint: How is boiling different from evaporation?
k6l10.expl: Evaporation occurs only at the surface at any temperature; boiling occurs throughout the liquid at a fixed boiling point.

k6l11.q: What percentage of air volume is oxygen?
k6l11.hint: Look at the pie chart of air composition.
k6l11.expl: Air consists of approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, and 1% carbon dioxide, water vapor, and other gases.

k6l11.q: Which gas has the largest volume percentage in normal air?

a.quiz: Nitrogen

k6l11.hint: It makes up more than three-quarters of the air.
k6l11.expl: Nitrogen accounts for about 78% of the air by volume, making it the most abundant gas.

opts: Water contains a small amount of dissolved oxygen

a.quiz: Water contains a small amount of dissolved oxygen

k6l11.hint: Oxygen is slightly soluble in water.
k6l11.expl: Although oxygen is only slightly soluble in water, dissolved oxygen allows fish and aquatic organisms to respire.

k6l11.q: In the burning candle experiment under a graduated glass jar, why does water rise about one-fifth of the jar height?
opts: Because water occupies the space of the consumed oxygen (about 21%)

a.quiz: Because water occupies the space of the consumed oxygen (about 21%)

k6l11.expl: Burning consumes oxygen (about 21% of air), while carbon dioxide is absorbed by limewater, causing liquid to rise ~1/5 of the jar.

k6l11.q: Which action helps reduce air pollution and keep the air clean?
opts: Using public transport, clean energy, and planting trees

a.quiz: Using public transport, clean energy, and planting trees

k6l11.expl: Using public transport, developing clean energy (solar, wind, water), and planting trees reduce toxic emissions and protect the air.

k6l11.q: Air consists of about 78% ___, 21% oxygen, and 1% other gases.

a.quiz: nitrogen

k6l11.sentence: Air consists of about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen.
k6l11.hint: The most abundant gas in Earth’s atmosphere.
k6l11.expl: Nitrogen makes up roughly 78% of the air volume.

k6l11.q: Toxic exhaust gases from factories and vehicles can react with water vapor to cause ___.

a.quiz: acid rain

k6l11.hint: Harmful rain that damages buildings and crops.
k6l11.expl: Pollutant gases dissolve in atmospheric water vapor to form acid rain.

k6l11.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k6l11.raw: Oxygen is essential for the respiration of living things and burning fuel.
k6l11.sentence: Oxygen is essential for the respiration of living things and burning fuel.
chunks: for the respiration of living things
k6l11.expl: Two key roles of oxygen are respiration and combustion.

k6l11.hint: Three items are clean renewable energy sources.
k6l11.expl: Burning coal releases smoke and carbon dioxide, causing air pollution.

k6l11.q: Divers, mountaineers, and astronauts carry oxygen tanks because those environments lack sufficient oxygen.
k6l11.hint: Think about breathing underwater, at high altitudes, or in space.
k6l11.expl: Humans need ~21% oxygen to breathe; underwater, high mountains, and space lack breathable oxygen.

k6l11.q: Find and correct the mistake: Oxygen makes up 78% of the air while nitrogen makes up 21%.

a.fix: Nitrogen makes up 78% of the air while oxygen makes up 21%.

k6l11.raw: Nitrogen makes up 78% of the air while oxygen makes up 21%.
k6l11.hint: Check the percentages of nitrogen and oxygen.
k6l11.expl: Air is approximately 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen by volume.

k6l12.q: Why are metal cooking pots usually fitted with wooden or plastic handles?
opts: Wood and plastic conduct heat very fast
Wood and plastic are poor heat conductors, preventing burns
Wood and plastic are heavier than metal

a.quiz: Wood and plastic are poor heat conductors, preventing burns

k6l12.hint: Think about holding a hot pot safely.
k6l12.expl: Wood and plastic conduct heat poorly (thermal insulators), keeping hands safe from burns while cooking.

k6l12.q: Which material is elastic, waterproof, and used to make car tires?

a.quiz: Rubber

k6l12.hint: Car tires need elasticity and water resistance.
k6l12.expl: Rubber is elastic, durable, waterproof, and non-conductive, making it ideal for vehicle tires.

k6l12.q: In the electrical conductivity test, what happens when a plastic ruler is clipped into the circuit?
opts: The bulb does not light up because plastic is an electrical insulator

a.quiz: The bulb does not light up because plastic is an electrical insulator

k6l12.hint: Does plastic allow electricity to pass through?
k6l12.expl: Plastic does not conduct electricity, so the circuit remains open and the bulb stays off.

k6l12.q: Which property describes glass used for windows and flower vases?

a.quiz: Transparent and brittle

k6l12.hint: Light passes through glass, yet it breaks easily if dropped.
k6l12.expl: Glass is transparent (lets light pass through), corrosion-resistant, hard, but brittle and fragile.

k6l12.q: What do the three Rs in the 3R waste management cycle stand for?

a.quiz: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle

k6l12.hint: Three actions to minimize household waste.
k6l12.expl: The 3R cycle stands for Reduce (giảm thiểu), Reuse (tái sử dụng), and Recycle (tái chế).

k6l12.q: Electrical wires are covered with ___ to prevent electric shock.

a.quiz: plastic

k6l12.sentence: Electrical wires are covered with plastic.
k6l12.hint: Choose a material that does not conduct electricity.
k6l12.expl: Plastic is an electrical insulator used to coat metal wires safely.

k6l12.q: When a metal spoon and a wooden spoon are placed in hot water, the ___ spoon gets hot much faster.

a.quiz: metal

k6l12.expl: Metals are good thermal conductors, so heat travels quickly up the metal spoon.

k6l12.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k6l12.raw: Metals conduct electricity and heat well, so they are used for wires and pots.
k6l12.sentence: Metals conduct electricity and heat well, so they are used for wires and pots.
k6l12.expl: This connects the properties of metals to their everyday uses.

k6l12.hint: Three items are poor conductors of electricity (insulators).
k6l12.expl: Copper is a metal that conducts electricity well, whereas plastic, rubber, and wood are insulators.

k6l12.q: Single-use plastic bottles marked with symbol 1 (PETE) should not be reused repeatedly because harmful chemicals may dissolve.
k6l12.hint: Check the warning about symbol 1 (PETE) in the textbook.
k6l12.expl: PETE (1) bottles are designed for single use; reusing them many times increases the risk of chemical leaching.

k6l12.q: Find and correct the mistake: Glass conducts electricity well and is very flexible like rubber.

a.fix: Glass does not conduct electricity and is hard but brittle.

k6l12.raw: Glass does not conduct electricity and is hard but brittle.
k6l12.hint: Think about what happens if you drop a glass cup.
k6l12.expl: Glass is an electrical and thermal insulator, transparent, hard, and brittle—not flexible.

k6l13.q: What is the main chemical component of limestone?

a.quiz: Calcium carbonate

k6l13.hint: Think about the white or gray rock that fizzes with acid.
k6l13.expl: Limestone consists primarily of calcium carbonate, along with small amounts of clay or sand impurities.

k6l13.q: What happens when drops of hydrochloric acid are placed on limestone?
opts: Gas bubbles appear on the surface

a.quiz: Gas bubbles appear on the surface

k6l13.hint: Calcium carbonate reacts with acid to release gas.
k6l13.expl: Hydrochloric acid reacts with calcium carbonate in limestone, producing visible carbon dioxide gas bubbles.

k6l13.q: Which metal is produced from bauxite ore?

a.quiz: Aluminum

k6l13.hint: Vietnam has large deposits of this ore in the Central Highlands (Tây Nguyên).
k6l13.expl: Bauxite ore is refined to produce aluminum, a lightweight metal used in aircraft, cars, and construction.

k6l13.q: Which combination of raw materials is heated to produce clinker for making cement?

a.quiz: Clay, limestone, and sand

k6l13.hint: Check the rotary kiln diagram in the textbook.
k6l13.expl: Clay, limestone, and sand are roasted in a rotary kiln to form clinker, which is then ground into cement.

k6l13.q: Why must natural ores be mined and used wisely?
opts: Because natural ores are finite, non-renewable resources and mining affects the environment
Because ores are made of plastic

a.quiz: Because natural ores are finite, non-renewable resources and mining affects the environment

k6l13.expl: Natural ore deposits are non-renewable and finite, so rational extraction protects national resources and the environment.

k6l13.q: ___ is heated in a kiln to produce quicklime and is also used to make cement.

a.quiz: Limestone

k6l13.sentence: Limestone is heated to produce quicklime.
k6l13.hint: This rock is rich in calcium carbonate.
k6l13.expl: Limestone is roasted to make quicklime and mixed with clay and sand to produce cement.

k6l13.q: People extract aluminum from ___ ore for aircraft, cars, and electrical engineering.

a.quiz: bauxite

k6l13.hint: Remember the ore mined in Tây Nguyên.
k6l13.expl: Bauxite is the main ore used to manufacture aluminum.

k6l13.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k6l13.raw: Natural raw materials include rocks, soil, ores, crude oil, and sugarcane.
k6l13.sentence: Natural raw materials include rocks, soil, ores, crude oil, and sugarcane.
k6l13.expl: This lists major natural raw materials.

k6l13.hint: Three items are natural raw materials.
k6l13.expl: Lipstick is a manufactured cosmetic product, whereas limestone, bauxite, and crude oil are natural raw materials.

k6l13.q: When hydrochloric acid is dropped onto limestone, gas bubbles form and limestone can be scratched by an iron nail.
k6l13.hint: Recall the two tests on limestone in the textbook.
k6l13.expl: Limestone is softer than an iron nail (so it scratches) and reacts with hydrochloric acid to release gas bubbles.

k6l13.q: Find and correct the mistake: Iron ore is used to produce aluminum, while bauxite ore is used to produce cast iron and steel.

a.fix: Bauxite ore is used to produce aluminum, while iron ore is used to produce cast iron and steel.

k6l13.raw: Bauxite ore is used to produce aluminum, while iron ore is used to produce cast iron and steel.
k6l13.hint: Swap the two ores to match their metals.
k6l13.expl: Bauxite yields aluminum, whereas iron ore yields cast iron and steel.

opts: A substance that burns and releases a large amount of heat

a.quiz: A substance that burns and releases a large amount of heat

k6l14.hint: Think about what happens when wood, gas, or gasoline burns.
k6l14.expl: Fuels are combustible substances that release considerable heat when burned for cooking, heating, or powering engines.

k6l14.q: Which group contains ONLY fossil fuels?
opts: Coal, crude oil, and natural gas

a.quiz: Coal, crude oil, and natural gas

k6l14.hint: These fuels formed over millions of years from ancient plants without oxygen.
k6l14.expl: Coal, crude oil, and natural gas are non-renewable fossil fuels formed millions of years ago.

k6l14.q: Which fossil fuel produces the most pollutants when burned because it contains many impurities?

a.quiz: Coal

k6l14.hint: This solid fuel is mined heavily in Quang Ninh.
k6l14.expl: Coal contains many impurities and releases significant toxic gases and dust when burned, making it the most polluting fossil fuel.

k6l14.q: Which products are obtained by distilling crude oil?

a.quiz: Gasoline, kerosene, and fuel gas

k6l14.hint: Think about liquid and gas fuels refined from petroleum.
k6l14.expl: Distilling crude oil separates it into useful fuels such as gasoline, kerosene, and fuel gas.

k6l14.q: Which energy sources are renewable alternatives to fossil fuels?
opts: Solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal energy

a.quiz: Solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal energy

k6l14.hint: Choose sources that naturally replenish and do not run out.
k6l14.expl: Hydroelectric, geothermal, solar, wind, and bioenergy are renewable energy sources that help ensure energy security.

k6l14.q: ___ is a liquid fuel distilled from crude oil and used to run car engines.

a.quiz: Gasoline

k6l14.sentence: Gasoline is a liquid fuel used to run car engines.
k6l14.hint: Think of the fuel pumped into cars and motorbikes.
k6l14.expl: Gasoline is a volatile liquid fuel refined from crude oil for vehicles.

k6l14.q: Solar, wind, and hydro power are ___ energy sources that help replace fossil fuels.

a.quiz: renewable

k6l14.hint: These clean energy sources do not run out.
k6l14.expl: Renewable energy sources replenish naturally and reduce reliance on finite fossil fuels.

k6l14.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k6l14.raw: Fuels exist in three states: solid coal, liquid gasoline, and natural gas.
k6l14.sentence: Fuels exist in three states: solid coal, liquid gasoline, and natural gas.
k6l14.expl: Fuels can be solid, liquid, or gas.
Wind power is a clean renewable energy source, whereas coal, crude oil, and natural gas are fossil fuels.

k6l14.q: Most fuels are lighter than water (except coal) and insoluble in water (except alcohol).
k6l14.hint: Check the physical properties of fuels in the textbook.
k6l14.expl: Most liquid fuels like gasoline and kerosene float on water and do not dissolve in water.

k6l14.q: Find and correct the mistake: Fossil fuels are renewable resources that form in just a few days.

a.fix: Fossil fuels are non-renewable resources that take millions of years to form.
