k6l54.q: The four outer planets—Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and ___—are large and cold.

a.quiz: Neptune

k6l54.hint: The farthest planet from the Sun.
k6l54.expl: Neptune is the eighth planet and farthest from the Sun at 30.07 AU.

k6l54.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k6l54.raw: Mercury is closest to the Sun (0.39 AU) and Neptune is farthest from the Sun (30.07 AU).
k6l54.sentence: Mercury is closest to the Sun (0.39 AU) and Neptune is farthest from the Sun (30.07 AU).
chunks: Mercury is closest to the Sun
k6l54.expl: This contrasts the nearest and farthest planets.

k6l54.hint: Three items are inner planets of the Solar System.
k6l54.expl: Jupiter is an outer gas giant planet, whereas Mercury, Venus, and Mars are inner planets.

k6l54.q: Looking directly at the Sun with the naked eye is dangerous and can harm your eyes.
k6l54.hint: Check the "Lưu ý" box on page 187.
k6l54.expl: Never look straight at the Sun; astronomers use specialized instruments/filters.

k6l54.q: Find and correct the mistake: All eight planets take the exact same 365.2 days to orbit the Sun regardless of distance.

a.fix: Planets at different distances from the Sun have different orbital periods (e.g., Mercury 88 days, Earth 365.2 days, Neptune 60,152 days).

k6l54.raw: Planets at different distances from the Sun have different orbital periods (e.g., Mercury 88 days, Earth 365.2 days, Neptune 60,152 days).
k6l54.hint: Check the orbital periods in the tables on pages 188–189.
k6l54.expl: Orbital periods differ across planets (88 days for Mercury up to 60,152 days for Neptune).

k6l55.q: What is the Milky Way (Ngân Hà), and what shape does it have when viewed perpendicular from above (Figure 55.1)?
opts: A spiral galaxy with 4 main spiral arms containing hundreds of billions of gravitational-bound celestial bodies, including our Solar System
A tiny square box 1 meter wide
A single solid rock orbiting the Moon in 1 hour
An empty void with no stars at all

a.quiz: A spiral galaxy with 4 main spiral arms containing hundreds of billions of gravitational-bound celestial bodies, including our Solar System

k6l55.hint: Check section I and Figure 55.1 on page 190.
k6l55.expl: The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy with four main spiral arms and hundreds of billions of celestial bodies bound by gravity.

k6l55.q: Where is our Solar System located within the Milky Way, and how far is it from the galactic center?
opts: Near the edge of a spiral arm, about 26,000 light-years from the center of the Milky Way
At the exact center of the universe 1 km away
Outside all galaxies in empty space
Inside a single grain of sand on Earth

a.quiz: Near the edge of a spiral arm, about 26,000 light-years from the center of the Milky Way

k6l55.expl: Our Solar System lies near the outer edge of a spiral arm, roughly 26,000 light-years from the Milky Way’s center.

k6l55.q: How long does it take the Sun to complete one orbit around the center of the Milky Way even at ~220,000 m/s?

a.quiz: About 230 million years

k6l55.expl: Even moving at ~220,000 m/s, the Sun takes about 230 million years to orbit once around the Milky Way’s center.

k6l55.q: What is a light-year (năm ánh sáng), and roughly how many kilometers is 1 light-year according to footnote (1) on page 190?
opts: Distance light travels in 1 year at ~300,000 km/s, roughly 95 trillion km
The weight of an elephant in tons

a.quiz: Distance light travels in 1 year at ~300,000 km/s, roughly 95 trillion km

k6l55.expl: One light-year is the distance light travels in one year, approximately 95 trillion km.

k6l55.q: What are observatories (đài thiên văn, Figures 55.4–55.5) used for, and name two observatories in Vietnam shown in the lesson?
opts: Facilities equipped with telescopes and instruments to observe/study celestial objects; Hoa Lac Observatory and Nha Trang Observatory (VNSC)

a.quiz: Facilities equipped with telescopes and instruments to observe/study celestial objects; Hoa Lac Observatory and Nha Trang Observatory (VNSC)

k6l55.expl: Observatories use telescopes and astronomical instruments to observe celestial bodies; Vietnam has Hoa Lac and Nha Trang observatories under VNSC.

k6l55.q: Seen from above perpendicular to its plane, the Milky Way has a ___ shape with four main arms.

a.quiz: spiral

k6l55.sentence: The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy.
k6l55.expl: The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy with four main spiral arms.

k6l55.q: Our Solar System is about 26,000 ___ from the center of the Milky Way.

a.quiz: light-years

k6l55.expl: Distance from the Solar System to the Milky Way center is about 26,000 light-years.

k6l55.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k6l55.raw: The universe contains trillions of galaxies with different shapes beyond the Milky Way.
k6l55.sentence: The universe contains trillions of galaxies with different shapes beyond the Milky Way.
k6l55.expl: This states that there are trillions of galaxies in the universe.

k6l55.hint: Three items are observatories or space observation facilities in Lesson 55.
k6l55.expl: A toaster is a household kitchen appliance, whereas Nha Trang Observatory, Hoa Lac Observatory, and telescopes are used in astronomy.

k6l55.q: If the Solar System were the size of a coin, the Milky Way would be as large as an entire continent.
k6l55.hint: Check the size comparison in section II on page 191.
k6l55.expl: The Solar System is tiny compared with the vast Milky Way.

k6l55.q: Find and correct the mistake: The Milky Way is the only galaxy in the entire universe and has a diameter of only 5 meters.

a.fix: The Milky Way is one of trillions of galaxies in the universe and has a diameter of about 100,000 light-years.

k6l55.raw: The Milky Way is one of trillions of galaxies in the universe and has a diameter of about 100,000 light-years.
k6l55.expl: The Milky Way is ~100,000 light-years across, and there are trillions of galaxies in the universe.

k7l1.q: What should you do if experimental results do not match your prediction in natural inquiry?
opts: Ignore the data and copy another group
Go back to step 2 to revise the prediction and re-test

a.quiz: Go back to step 2 to revise the prediction and re-test

k7l1.hint: Check the feedback arrow in the 5-step diagram.
k7l1.expl: If results do not support the prediction, return to step 2 to re-analyze, form a new prediction, and test again.

k7l1.q: Which process skill uses data and prior knowledge to discover new relationships between phenomena?

a.quiz: Linking (liên kết)

k7l1.hint: Think about connecting water cycle stages to climate and ecosystems.
k7l1.expl: Linking uses observed data and existing knowledge to identify relationships among objects or phenomena.

k7l1.q: On a digital timer in Grade 7 experiments, which mode measures time as an object passes from photogate A to photogate B?

a.quiz: Mode A<->B

k7l1.hint: Look at the MODE selector description in section III.2.
k7l1.expl: Mode A<->B opens the timer when the object passes photogate A and stops it at photogate B, displaying time interval Δt.

k7l1.q: Which button resets the digital timer display back to zero?

a.quiz: RESET

k7l1.hint: Look at button (3) on the front panel of the digital timer.
k7l1.expl: Pressing RESET returns the digital timer to its initial zero state.

k7l1.q: What are the main sections of a standard lab report in the textbook?
opts: Only a title and a drawing
Purpose, preparation, procedure, results, and answers to questions

a.quiz: Purpose, preparation, procedure, results, and answers to questions

k7l1.hint: Check the lab report template in section IV.1.
k7l1.expl: A lab report includes: 1. Purpose, 2. Preparation, 3. Procedure, 4. Results (data table, calculation, conclusion), and 5. Questions.

k7l1.q: A ___ uses infrared transmitter D1 and receiver D2 to control a digital timer.

a.quiz: photogate

k7l1.sentence: A photogate controls a digital timer.
k7l1.hint: It acts as an electronic switch for time measurement.
k7l1.expl: A photogate sends electric signals to open and close the digital timer.

k7l1.q: Using models and calculations to estimate future outcomes is called quantitative ___.

a.quiz: prediction

k7l1.hint: It is process skill number 4 in section II.4.
k7l1.expl: Prediction states what will happen based on observations, knowledge, reasoning, or models.

k7l1.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k7l1.raw: Natural inquiry involves five steps from proposing a problem to reporting results.
k7l1.sentence: Natural inquiry involves five steps from proposing a problem to reporting results.
k7l1.expl: This summarizes the 5-step scientific inquiry cycle.

k7l1.hint: Three items are process skills in natural science.
k7l1.expl: A digital timer is a measuring instrument, whereas observation, classification, and prediction are process skills.

k7l1.q: Sliding friction force on a wooden block does not change merely because its contact area with the table changes.
k7l1.hint: Check the example experiment in Figure 1.1.
k7l1.expl: In the textbook’s sliding friction example, changing contact area (12x6 cm vs. 12x3 cm) does not change sliding friction force.

k7l1.q: Find and correct the mistake: Pressing RESET on the digital timer sets the working mode to A<->B.

a.fix: Pressing RESET returns the digital timer to zero, while MODE selects the working mode such as A<->B.

k7l1.raw: Pressing RESET returns the digital timer to zero, while MODE selects the working mode such as A<->B.
k7l1.expl: RESET resets the display to 0.000, whereas MODE selects how the photogates control timing.

k7l2.q: Which particles make up the atomic nucleus?

a.quiz: Protons and neutrons

k7l2.hint: Think about the center of the atom.
k7l2.expl: The nucleus consists of positively charged protons (p) and uncharged neutrons (n).

k7l2.q: Why is an atom electrically neutral?
opts: Because it has no charged particles at all
Because the number of protons (+1) equals the number of electrons (-1)
Because electrons have a mass of 100 amu

a.quiz: Because the number of protons (+1) equals the number of electrons (-1)

k7l2.expl: Each proton has charge +1 and each electron has charge -1; equal numbers make the atom electrically neutral.

k7l2.q: According to Bohr’s model, what is the maximum number of electrons in the first (innermost) shell and second shell?

a.quiz: First: 2; Second: 8

k7l2.hint: The inner shell is closest to the nucleus and holds the fewest electrons.
k7l2.expl: The first electron shell holds at most 2 electrons, and the second shell holds at most 8 electrons.

k7l2.q: Why can the mass of the nucleus be taken as the approximate mass of an atom?
opts: Because electrons are heavier than protons
Because a proton and neutron are each ~1 amu while an electron is ~0.00055 amu

a.quiz: Because a proton and neutron are each ~1 amu while an electron is ~0.00055 amu

k7l2.hint: Compare the mass of a proton/neutron with an electron in amu.
k7l2.expl: A proton (~1 amu) and neutron (~1 amu) are about 1,800 times heavier than an electron (~0.00055 amu), so atomic mass is concentrated in the nucleus.

k7l2.q: In a carbon atom with 6 protons and 6 neutrons, how many electrons are in the outer shell?

a.quiz: 4 electrons

k7l2.hint: Carbon has 6 electrons total: 2 in the first shell and the rest in the second (outer) shell.
k7l2.expl: A neutral carbon atom has 6 electrons: 2 in the inner shell and 4 in the outer shell (total 6).

k7l2.q: A ___ carries no electric charge and is located inside the atomic nucleus.

a.quiz: neutron

k7l2.sentence: A neutron has no electric charge.
k7l2.hint: Think of the neutral particle in the nucleus.
k7l2.expl: Neutrons are uncharged particles inside the nucleus alongside positively charged protons.

k7l2.q: The nuclear charge number Z equals the total number of ___ in the nucleus.

a.quiz: protons

k7l2.expl: The number of protons in the nucleus defines the nuclear charge number Z.

k7l2.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k7l2.raw: An atom is electrically neutral because the number of protons equals the number of electrons.
k7l2.sentence: An atom is electrically neutral because the number of protons equals the number of electrons.
k7l2.expl: This explains electrical neutrality of an atom.
An electron shell is a region/level around the nucleus, whereas proton, neutron, and electron are subatomic particles.

k7l2.q: Outer-shell electrons determine the chemical properties of an atom.
k7l2.hint: Check section III.2 on atomic shells.
k7l2.expl: Electrons in the outermost shell govern how an atom interacts and forms chemical bonds.

k7l2.q: Find and correct the mistake: An electron carries a +1 charge and weighs about 1 amu, while a proton has a -1 charge.

a.fix: A proton carries a +1 charge (~1 amu), while an electron carries a -1 charge (~0.00055 amu).

k7l2.raw: A proton carries a +1 charge (~1 amu), while an electron carries a -1 charge (~0.00055 amu).
k7l2.hint: Check the charges and masses in sections III–IV.
k7l2.expl: Protons are positive (+1, ~1 amu); neutrons are neutral (0, ~1 amu); electrons are negative (-1, ~0.00055 amu).

k7l3.q: What determines whether atoms belong to the same chemical element?
opts: Having the same number of protons in the nucleus
Having the exact same color and size
Having the same number of neutrons only
Being found in the same bottle

a.quiz: Having the same number of protons in the nucleus

k7l3.expl: Atoms with the same number of protons belong to the same chemical element, even if neutron numbers differ.

k7l3.q: Which rule applies when writing a two-letter chemical symbol?
opts: First letter is capitalized and second letter is lowercase (e.g., Na, He, Mg)
Symbols are written with numbers only

a.quiz: First letter is capitalized and second letter is lowercase (e.g., Na, He, Mg)

k7l3.hint: Check section II.2 on writing chemical symbols.
k7l3.expl: A chemical symbol consists of one or two letters: the first is uppercase and the second is lowercase.

k7l3.q: Which element has atomic number 8, symbol O, and atomic mass ~16 amu?

a.quiz: Oxygen

k7l3.expl: Oxygen has atomic number Z = 8, symbol O, and atomic mass ~16 amu.

k7l3.q: Which element in the first 20 elements has an atomic mass of about 35.5 amu and symbol Cl?

a.quiz: Chlorine (Z = 17)

k7l3.expl: Chlorine (Z = 17, symbol Cl) has a rounded atomic mass of 35.5 amu.

k7l3.q: Which four elements make up about 96% of the human body’s weight?

a.quiz: Oxygen (65%), carbon (18.5%), hydrogen (9.5%), and nitrogen (3%)

k7l3.hint: Check the pie chart in Figure 3.2.
k7l3.expl: Oxygen, carbon, hydrogen, and nitrogen together account for roughly 96% of human body mass.

k7l3.q: The ___ number equals the number of protons in an atom’s nucleus.

a.quiz: atomic

k7l3.sentence: The atomic number equals the proton count.
k7l3.hint: Each element has its own unique number.
k7l3.expl: The atomic number is equal to the number of protons in the nucleus.

k7l3.q: The chemical symbol of potassium is ___, coming from its Latin name kalium.

a.quiz: K

k7l3.hint: Do not confuse potassium with phosphorus (P).
k7l3.expl: Potassium has symbol K from Latin kalium, whereas phosphorus has symbol P.

k7l3.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k7l3.raw: Atoms with the same number of protons belong to the same chemical element.
k7l3.sentence: Atoms with the same number of protons belong to the same chemical element.
chunks: with the same number of protons

k7l3.hint: Three items are elements among Z = 1..20 with 1-letter symbols.
k7l3.expl: Magnesium (Mg, Z = 12) has a two-letter symbol, whereas H, N, and O have one-letter symbols.

k7l3.q: Atoms of the same chemical element can have different numbers of neutrons.
k7l3.hint: Think about oxygen atoms with 8 protons and 8, 9, or 10 neutrons.
k7l3.expl: Same proton number defines the element, while neutron counts can vary.

k7l3.q: Find and correct the mistake: Sodium has chemical symbol SO and atomic number 16.

a.fix: Sodium has chemical symbol Na and atomic number 11 (atomic mass ~23 amu).

k7l3.raw: Sodium has chemical symbol Na and atomic number 11 (atomic mass ~23 amu).
k7l3.hint: Check Table 3.1 for sodium and sulfur.
k7l3.expl: Sodium is Na (Z = 11, ~23 amu); sulfur is S (Z = 16, ~32 amu).

k7l4.q: What do elements in the same period (row) of the periodic table have in common?
opts: The same number of electron shells

a.quiz: The same number of electron shells

k7l4.hint: Period number = number of electron shells.
k7l4.expl: Elements in the same period have the same number of electron shells, ordered by increasing nuclear charge from left to right.

k7l4.q: Which group in the periodic table contains the noble gases (khí hiếm)?

a.quiz: Group VIIIA

k7l4.hint: Look at the far-right column on page 25.
k7l4.expl: Noble gases (such as He, Ne, and Ar) are located in group VIIIA and have stable outer electron shells.

k7l4.q: How many periods are in the current periodic table, and which ones are short periods?
opts: 7 periods total; periods 1, 2, and 3 are short periods
5 periods total; all are long periods
2 periods total; both are noble gases

a.quiz: 7 periods total; periods 1, 2, and 3 are short periods

k7l4.hint: Check section II.2 on periods 1 to 7.
k7l4.expl: There are 7 periods (rows): periods 1, 2, and 3 are short periods, while periods 4, 5, 6, and 7 are long periods.

k7l4.q: Why do noble gas atoms rarely undergo chemical changes?
opts: They have unstable outer shells with 1 electron
They have a stable outer electron shell (8 electrons, or 2 for He)

a.quiz: They have a stable outer electron shell (8 electrons, or 2 for He)

k7l4.hint: Look at section III.3 on noble gases.
k7l4.expl: Noble gases have full, stable outer electron shells (2 for He; 8 for Ne, Ar, etc.), making them chemically unreactive.

k7l4.q: Which of the following elements is a nonmetal in the periodic table?

a.quiz: Oxygen (O)

k7l4.hint: Nonmetals are mostly in the upper-right of the periodic table.
k7l4.expl: Oxygen (O, Z = 8, period 2, group VIA) is a nonmetal, whereas Al, Cu, and Ca are metals.

k7l4.q: An ___ shows atomic number, chemical symbol, element name, and atomic mass.

a.quiz: element cell

k7l4.sentence: An element cell shows key element data.
k7l4.hint: It is one box in the periodic table.
k7l4.expl: Each element cell (ô nguyên tố) presents key data for a chemical element.

k7l4.q: Group VIIA is also known as the ___ group.

a.quiz: halogen

k7l4.expl: Group VIIA is called the halogen group and consists of typical nonmetals (except Ts).

k7l4.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k7l4.raw: Elements in the same period have the same number of electron shells.
k7l4.sentence: Elements in the same period have the same number of electron shells.
k7l4.expl: This states the rule for a period.

k7l4.hint: Three items are noble gases in group VIIIA.
k7l4.expl: Chlorine (Cl) is a halogen in group VIIA, whereas helium (He), neon (Ne), and argon (Ar) are noble gases.

k7l4.q: Neon (Ne) is at atomic number 10, period 2, and group VIIIA.
k7l4.hint: Check the periodic table on page 25.
k7l4.expl: Neon has Z = 10, 2 electron shells (period 2), and 8 outer electrons (group VIIIA).

k7l4.q: Find and correct the mistake: In 1869, Mendeleev arranged elements strictly by increasing nuclear charge rather than atomic mass.

a.fix: In 1869, Mendeleev arranged elements by increasing atomic mass, while modern tables use increasing nuclear charge.

k7l4.raw: In 1869, Mendeleev arranged elements by increasing atomic mass, while modern tables use increasing nuclear charge.
k7l4.hint: Check the historical note on page 24.
k7l4.expl: Mendeleev’s 1869 table ordered elements by atomic mass; later scientists established nuclear charge as the organizing basis.

k7l5.q: Which of the following is a simple substance (đơn chất)?
opts: Carbon dioxide (made of C and O)

a.quiz: Copper or nitrogen gas

k7l5.hint: A simple substance contains only one chemical element.
k7l5.expl: Copper (Cu) and nitrogen (N2) consist of only one chemical element, so they are simple substances.

k7l5.q: Which of the following is a compound (hợp chất)?

a.quiz: Water (H and O)

k7l5.hint: A compound consists of two or more chemical elements.
k7l5.expl: Water contains hydrogen and oxygen (two elements), making it a compound.

k7l5.q: What is the molecular mass of nitrogen (N2), given atomic mass of N is 14 amu?

a.quiz: 28 amu

k7l5.hint: Two nitrogen atoms are bonded together: 2 × 14.
k7l5.expl: A nitrogen molecule has two N atoms, so its molecular mass is 2 × 14 = 28 amu.

k7l5.q: What is the molecular mass of methane (CH4), given C = 12 amu and H = 1 amu?

a.quiz: 16 amu

k7l5.hint: One carbon atom (12) plus four hydrogen atoms (4 × 1).
k7l5.expl: Methane has 1 C atom and 4 H atoms, so its molecular mass is 12×1 + 1×4 = 16 amu.

a.quiz: Glucose, water, and carbon dioxide

k7l5.hint: Each substance must contain at least two elements.
k7l5.expl: Glucose (C, H, O), water (H, O), and carbon dioxide (C, O) are all compounds.

k7l5.q: A ___ is made of two or more chemical elements bonded together.

a.quiz: compound

k7l5.hint: Water and carbon dioxide are examples.
k7l5.expl: A compound consists of two or more different chemical elements.

k7l5.q: Molecular mass is measured in ___ and equals the sum of atomic masses in a molecule.

a.quiz: amu

k7l5.hint: Same atomic mass unit from Lesson 2.
k7l5.expl: Molecular mass in amu is the sum of the masses of all atoms in the molecule.

k7l5.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k7l5.raw: A simple substance is made of one chemical element, while a compound is made of two or more.
k7l5.sentence: A simple substance is made of one chemical element, while a compound is made of two or more.
chunks: is made of one chemical element,
is made of two or more
k7l5.expl: This contrasts simple substances and compounds.
Water is a compound (H and O), whereas copper, helium, and ozone are made of one element.

k7l5.q: Carbon can form different simple forms such as diamond, graphite, and wood charcoal.
k7l5.hint: Check the note on carbon simple substances on page 33.
k7l5.expl: A single element like carbon can form different simple substance forms such as diamond and graphite.

k7l5.q: Find and correct the mistake: A molecule of water consists of two oxygen atoms and one hydrogen atom with mass 33 amu.

a.fix: A water molecule consists of one oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms with molecular mass 18 amu.

k7l5.raw: A water molecule consists of one oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms with molecular mass 18 amu.
k7l5.hint: Count H and O atoms in water.
k7l5.expl: Water has 2 H atoms (2×1 = 2 amu) and 1 O atom (16 amu), totaling 18 amu.

k7l6.q: How is an ionic bond (liên kết ion) formed?
opts: By sharing electrons equally with no charges
By electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions (positive and negative ions)
By splitting a nucleus into two

a.quiz: By electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions (positive and negative ions)

k7l6.hint: Positive ions and negative ions attract each other.
k7l6.expl: Transfer of electrons creates positive and negative ions, and their opposite charges attract to form an ionic bond.

k7l6.q: In forming MgO (Figure 6.3), how many electrons does a magnesium (Mg) atom lose?

a.quiz: 2 electrons

k7l6.hint: Mg has 2 outer electrons and forms Mg2+.
k7l6.expl: Each Mg atom loses 2 outer electrons to form Mg2+, while oxygen gains 2 electrons to form O2-.

k7l6.q: How many shared electron pairs are formed in an oxygen molecule (O2) in Figure 6.5?

a.quiz: 2 shared pairs

k7l6.hint: Each O atom has 6 outer electrons and shares 2 electrons to reach 8.
k7l6.expl: Each oxygen atom contributes 2 electrons, forming two shared electron pairs in O2.

k7l6.q: Which property is typical of an ionic compound like sodium chloride (NaCl)?
opts: Solid at room temperature, hard to melt/vaporize, and conducts electricity when dissolved in water
Always a gas at room temperature

a.quiz: Solid at room temperature, hard to melt/vaporize, and conducts electricity when dissolved in water

k7l6.hint: Check the note on ionic compounds on page 37.
k7l6.expl: Ionic compounds like NaCl are typically solids with high melting/boiling points whose aqueous solutions conduct electricity.

k7l6.q: Which of the following is a covalent substance (chất cộng hóa trị)?

a.quiz: Water (H2O) or carbon dioxide (CO2)

k7l6.hint: Covalent substances involve shared electron pairs.
k7l6.expl: Water and carbon dioxide consist of atoms joined by covalent bonds (shared electron pairs).

k7l6.q: A neutral atom becomes a charged ___ when it loses or gains electrons.

a.quiz: ion

k7l6.sentence: Atoms form ions by losing or gaining electrons.
k7l6.expl: Losing or gaining electrons turns a neutral atom into a positive or negative ion.

k7l6.q: In a hydrogen molecule (H2), two H atoms share ___ electron pair.

a.quiz: one

k7l6.hint: Each H atom has 1 electron and shares 1 to reach 2 like helium.
k7l6.expl: Each H atom contributes 1 electron to form one shared electron pair.

k7l6.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k7l6.raw: An ionic bond is formed by attraction between oppositely charged ions.
k7l6.sentence: An ionic bond is formed by attraction between oppositely charged ions.

k7l6.expl: Sodium chloride (NaCl) is an ionic compound, whereas water, ammonia, and carbon dioxide are covalent substances.

k7l6.q: Covalent substances can be gases, liquids, or solids and generally have lower melting and boiling points than ionic compounds.
k7l6.expl: Covalent substances exist in all three states and usually melt and boil at lower temperatures than ionic solids.

k7l6.q: Find and correct the mistake: In NaCl formation, chlorine loses an electron to become Cl+ and sodium gains it to become Na-.

a.fix: Sodium (Na) loses an electron to become Na+, and chlorine (Cl) gains it to become Cl-.

k7l6.raw: Sodium (Na) loses an electron to become Na+, and chlorine (Cl) gains it to become Cl-.
k7l6.hint: Metals lose electrons to become positive ions; nonmetals gain electrons.
k7l6.expl: Na loses 1 electron to form Na+ (like Ne) and Cl gains 1 electron to form Cl- (like Ar).

k7l7.q: What is the molecular mass of calcium carbonate (CaCO3), given Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16 amu?

a.quiz: 100 amu

k7l7.q: What is the chemical formula of the compound formed by sulfur (valence IV) and oxygen (valence II)?

a.quiz: SO2

k7l7.hint: x × IV = y × II => x/y = II/IV = 1/2.
k7l7.expl: Using the valence rule, x : y = 2 : 4 = 1 : 2, giving formula SO2.

k7l7.q: What is the chemical formula of potassium oxide formed by K (valence I) and O (valence II)?

a.quiz: KO

k7l7.expl: By the valence rule, x : y = 2 : 1, so the formula is K2O (note: option B is K2O).

k7l7.q: In a chemical formula, how is a subscript equal to 1 written?
opts: Written as subscript 1 next to the symbol

a.quiz: Omitted (not written)

k7l7.hint: Check section I on writing chemical formulas.

k7l15.q: What is used in Figure 15.6 to model a light ray using a flashlight?
opts: A cardboard sheet with a small hole and a screen

a.quiz: A cardboard sheet with a small hole and a screen

k7l15.expl: Covering a flashlight with cardboard that has a small pinhole produces a narrow straight light strip on the screen as a ray model.

k7l15.q: Why does a wide light source create a less sharp shadow boundary than a narrow light source?
opts: Because a wide source forms both a dark region and a partial shadow receiving light from part of the source
Because light travels in zig-zags behind a wide source
Because obstacles disappear near wide lights
Because wide lights have no rays

a.quiz: Because a wide source forms both a dark region and a partial shadow receiving light from part of the source

k7l15.hint: Compare Figure 15.8 (narrow source) and Figure 15.9 (wide source).
k7l15.expl: A wide light source casts a dark shadow surrounded by a partial shadow (penumbra), making the shadow edge less sharp.

k7l15.q: During a solar eclipse (Figure 15.10), what do observers on Earth in the dark shadow vs. partial shadow see?
opts: Full solar eclipse in the dark shadow; partial solar eclipse in the partial shadow

a.quiz: Full solar eclipse in the dark shadow; partial solar eclipse in the partial shadow

k7l15.expl: In the dark shadow (umbral region) the Sun is blocked completely (total eclipse); in the partial shadow (penumbra) part of the Sun is visible (partial eclipse).

k7l15.q: A ___ cell converts light energy into electrical energy when illuminated.

a.quiz: solar

k7l15.sentence: A solar cell converts light into electricity.
k7l15.expl: A solar (photovoltaic) cell transforms light energy into electricity.

k7l15.q: The three common beam types in Figure 15.3 are parallel, convergent, and ___.

a.quiz: divergent

k7l15.hint: Rays spreading outward form this beam.
k7l15.expl: Light beams can be parallel, convergent (coming together), or divergent (spreading apart).

k7l15.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k7l15.raw: A light ray is represented by a straight line with an arrow showing direction.
k7l15.sentence: A light ray is represented by a straight line with an arrow showing direction.
chunks: is represented by a straight line
k7l15.expl: This states how a light ray is drawn.

k7l15.hint: Three items are types of light beams.
k7l15.expl: A solar eclipse is an astronomical alignment shadow event, whereas parallel, convergent, and divergent are types of light beams.

k7l15.q: A bottle of water left in sunlight warms up because light energy is converted into thermal energy.
k7l15.hint: Think about Question 2 on page 73 and solar water heaters.
k7l15.expl: Absorbing sunlight increases thermal energy, warming water in the bottle or solar heater.

k7l15.q: Find and correct the mistake: A narrow light source produces a blurry partial shadow with no sharp boundary, while a wide light source only makes a razor-sharp edge.

a.fix: A narrow light source forms a sharp-edged shadow, while a wide light source creates both a full shadow and a partial shadow with a less sharp boundary.

k7l15.raw: A narrow light source forms a sharp-edged shadow, while a wide light source creates both a full shadow and a partial shadow with a less sharp boundary.
k7l15.expl: A small/narrow source casts a sharp shadow; a wide source produces a partial shadow (penumbra) around the dark core.

k7l16.q: According to the law of reflection of light, what is true about the angle of reflection (i') and angle of incidence (i)?
opts: Angle of reflection i' equals angle of incidence i
Angle of reflection is always twice the angle of incidence
The reflected ray leaves the plane of incidence

a.quiz: Angle of reflection i' equals angle of incidence i

k7l16.hint: State the second part of the law of reflection.
k7l16.expl: According to the law of reflection, the reflected ray lies in the plane of incidence and i' = i.

k7l16.q: If an incident ray hits a plane mirror at an angle of incidence i = 30°, what is the angle of reflection i'?
k7l16.expl: Since angle of reflection equals angle of incidence, i' = 30°.

k7l16.q: What is the normal line (pháp tuyến IN) at point of incidence I?
opts: A line parallel to the mirror
A line perpendicular (90°) to the mirror at point I

a.quiz: A line perpendicular (90°) to the mirror at point I

k7l16.expl: The normal IN is the line perpendicular to the reflecting surface at point of incidence I.

k7l16.q: What happens when parallel light rays strike an uneven, non-smooth surface (diffuse reflection)?
opts: They all stop and turn into solid lead
They form a single laser beam
They pass straight through opaque stone

a.quiz: They reflect in all directions

k7l16.hint: Check section III and Figure 16.4 on page 80.
k7l16.expl: Diffuse reflection occurs on non-smooth surfaces, scattering parallel incident rays in many directions so no clear mirror image is seen.

k7l16.q: In Figure 16.5, why do you see a clear reflection image on still lake water (16.5a) but not on rippled water (16.5b)?
opts: Still water is smooth so parallel rays reflect uniformly; rippled water is uneven so light scatters in many directions
Rippled water is made of wood

a.quiz: Still water is smooth so parallel rays reflect uniformly; rippled water is uneven so light scatters in many directions

k7l16.expl: A calm, smooth water surface reflects light uniformly, whereas ripples make the surface uneven and cause diffuse reflection.

k7l16.q: The line perpendicular to the mirror at the point of incidence I is called the ___.

a.quiz: normal

k7l16.sentence: The normal is perpendicular to the mirror.
k7l16.expl: The normal IN is drawn at 90° to the reflecting surface at point I.

k7l16.q: When parallel rays hit a non-smooth surface and reflect in all directions, it is called ___ reflection.

a.quiz: diffuse

k7l16.expl: Diffuse reflection scatters parallel incident rays in many directions.

k7l16.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k7l16.raw: The reflected ray lies in the plane of incidence, and the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.
k7l16.sentence: The reflected ray lies in the plane of incidence, and the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.
k7l16.expl: This states the law of reflection.

k7l16.hint: Three items are rays or angles in a reflection diagram.
k7l16.expl: Diffuse reflection is a type of surface reflection phenomenon, whereas incident ray, reflected ray, and angle of incidence are parts of a single ray diagram.

k7l16.q: If the right half of the graduated board in Figure 16.2 is rotated out of the plane of incidence, the reflected ray is not seen on that rotated half.
k7l16.hint: Think about Experiment II.1 step 1c(1) on page 79.
k7l16.expl: Because the reflected ray lies in the plane of incidence, rotating the right half out of that plane moves the board away from the ray.

k7l16.q: Find and correct the mistake: According to the law of reflection, if angle of incidence i is 45°, angle of reflection i' is 90°.

a.fix: According to the law of reflection, if angle of incidence i is 45°, angle of reflection i' is also 45°.

k7l16.raw: According to the law of reflection, if angle of incidence i is 45°, angle of reflection i' is also 45°.
k7l16.hint: Angle of reflection equals angle of incidence.
k7l16.expl: Since i' = i, a 45° angle of incidence produces a 45° angle of reflection.

k7l17.q: Can the image of an object formed by a plane mirror be caught on a screen (màn chắn)?
opts: No, because it is a virtual image (ảnh ảo)
Yes, because light rays pass through the solid mirror
Yes, if the screen is painted black

a.quiz: No, because it is a virtual image (ảnh ảo)

k7l17.hint: Check section II.1 and "EM ĐÃ HỌC" on page 85.
k7l17.expl: A plane-mirror image is virtual (formed where backward extensions of reflected rays meet), so it cannot be caught on a screen.

k7l17.q: How do the size of an image in a plane mirror and its distance to the mirror compare with the object?
opts: Image size equals object size, and image distance to mirror equals object distance to mirror
Image is twice as large and twice as far

a.quiz: Image size equals object size, and image distance to mirror equals object distance to mirror

k7l17.hint: Check experiment II.2 with two candles on page 83.
k7l17.expl: For a plane mirror, image size equals object size and image distance from the mirror equals object distance from the mirror.

k7l17.q: A person stands 4 m in front of a wall with a plane mirror. How far and in which direction must the person move to be 2 m from their image? (Question 1 on page 83)
opts: Move 1 m toward the mirror (distance to mirror becomes 3 m; image is 3 m behind -> total 6 m? Wait: if distance to mirror is d, distance to image is 2d; for 2d = 2 m, d = 1 m, so move 3 m toward the mirror)
Move 3 m toward the mirror (so distance to mirror becomes 1 m and distance to image becomes 2 m)
Move 4 m away from the mirror

a.quiz: Move 3 m toward the mirror (so distance to mirror becomes 1 m and distance to image becomes 2 m)

k7l17.hint: Distance between object and virtual image is 2 × (distance from object to mirror).
k7l17.expl: To be 2 m from the image, the person must be 1 m from the mirror (2 × 1 m = 2 m), so they move 3 m toward the mirror from 4 m away.

k7l17.q: Why is the word AMBULANCE written reversed on the front of an ambulance?
opts: So drivers ahead looking in their rear-view mirror see AMBULANCE clearly and yield quickly
To make the car go backward faster
Because English reads right to left on cars

a.quiz: So drivers ahead looking in their rear-view mirror see AMBULANCE clearly and yield quickly

k7l17.hint: Think about how a plane mirror reverses left and right.
k7l17.expl: Reversed lettering appears normal when viewed in a rear-view mirror, helping drivers read "AMBULANCE" quickly.

k7l17.q: How are backward extensions of reflected rays drawn when constructing virtual image S' in Figure 17.3?
opts: They are not drawn at all

a.quiz: With dashed lines

k7l17.expl: Extended reflected rays are drawn with dashed lines to show they are virtual rays meeting at S'.

k7l17.q: The image of an object in a plane mirror is a ___ image and cannot be caught on a screen.

a.quiz: virtual

k7l17.sentence: A plane mirror forms a virtual image.
k7l17.hint: Reflected rays do not actually converge on a screen.
k7l17.expl: A plane mirror forms a virtual image that cannot be projected onto a screen.

k7l17.q: A simple ___ uses two plane mirrors at 45° to see over or around obstacles.

a.quiz: periscope

k7l17.expl: A periscope reflects light off two mirrors to let you view hidden objects.

k7l17.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k7l17.raw: An object and its image formed by a plane mirror are symmetric across the mirror.
k7l17.sentence: An object and its image formed by a plane mirror are symmetric across the mirror.
k7l17.expl: This states symmetry across a plane mirror.

k7l17.hint: Three items are true statements about a plane-mirror image.
k7l17.expl: A plane-mirror image is virtual and cannot be caught on a screen.

k7l17.q: If an object is 5 cm in front of a plane mirror, its virtual image is 5 cm behind the mirror.
k7l17.expl: A plane-mirror image lies the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front of it.

k7l17.q: Find and correct the mistake: In a plane mirror, a 10 cm tall object forms a 20 cm tall image that can be projected onto a screen.

a.fix: In a plane mirror, a 10 cm tall object forms a 10 cm tall virtual image that cannot be caught on a screen.

k7l17.raw: In a plane mirror, a 10 cm tall object forms a 10 cm tall virtual image that cannot be caught on a screen.
k7l17.hint: Check size and screen property of a plane-mirror image.
k7l17.expl: Image size equals object size (10 cm) and is virtual, so it cannot be caught on a screen.

k7l18.q: Which materials are attracted by a magnet in Experiment II.1 (iron, steel, copper, aluminium, wood)?

a.quiz: Iron and steel

k7l18.hint: Magnets attract iron and some iron alloys (like steel).
k7l18.expl: Iron and steel are magnetic materials attracted by a magnet, whereas copper, aluminium, and wood are not attracted.

k7l18.q: In which direction does a freely suspended bar magnet or pivoted magnetic needle point at rest?

a.quiz: North–south

k7l18.hint: One end points toward geographic north and the other toward geographic south.
k7l18.expl: A balanced magnet or magnetic needle aligns along the north–south direction.

k7l18.q: What happens when the North pole of one magnet is brought close to the North pole of another magnet?

a.quiz: They repel (push apart)

k7l18.expl: Two like poles (N and N, or S and S) repel each other, while unlike poles (N and S) attract.

k7l18.q: Which colors and letters are commonly used to mark the North and South poles of a magnet?
opts: Red for North (N) and blue for South (S)
Blue for North (N) and red for South (S)

a.quiz: Red for North (N) and blue for South (S)

k7l18.hint: N stands for North and S stands for South.
k7l18.expl: Red typically marks the North pole (N) and blue marks the South pole (S).

k7l18.q: Which of the following is a practical use of magnets mentioned in the lesson?
opts: Removing iron scraps from food/grain or separating iron waste

a.quiz: Removing iron scraps from food/grain or separating iron waste

k7l18.expl: Magnets are used in iron-separator grids, removing tiny iron bits from food or eyes, and clearing scrap iron.

k7l18.q: When two magnets are placed near each other, unlike poles ___ and like poles repel.

a.quiz: attract

k7l18.hint: North and South pull toward each other.
k7l18.expl: Opposite/unlike magnetic poles attract, whereas like poles repel.

k7l18.q: A balanced magnetic needle at rest points along the ___-south direction.

a.quiz: north

k7l18.hint: One end points north and the other points south.
k7l18.expl: A free magnet aligns in the north–south direction.

k7l18.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k7l18.raw: When two magnets are brought close, unlike poles attract and like poles repel.
k7l18.sentence: When two magnets are brought close, unlike poles attract and like poles repel.
k7l18.expl: This states the interaction rule between two magnets.

k7l18.hint: Three items are non-magnetic materials in Experiment II.1.
k7l18.expl: Steel is a magnetic material attracted by magnets, whereas wood, copper, and aluminium are not.

k7l18.q: A test magnet (kim nam châm) placed near a magnet aligns along a definite direction due to magnetic force.
k7l18.hint: Check Experiment IV and "EM ĐÃ HỌC" on pages 88–89.
k7l18.expl: A test magnet placed near a magnet experiences magnetic force and takes a definite orientation.

k7l18.q: Find and correct the mistake: Two North poles of magnets attract each other, while a North pole and South pole repel.

a.fix: Two North poles repel each other, while a North pole and a South pole attract each other.

k7l18.raw: Two North poles repel each other, while a North pole and a South pole attract each other.
k7l18.hint: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
k7l18.expl: Like poles (N–N or S–S) repel, and unlike poles (N–S) attract.

k7l19.q: Where does a magnetic field (từ trường) exist according to Lesson 19?
opts: Around a magnet or a wire carrying an electric current
Only in empty space far from all magnets and currents
Inside a glass of water only

a.quiz: Around a magnet or a wire carrying an electric current

k7l19.hint: Both magnets and electric currents produce magnetic fields.
k7l19.expl: A magnetic field exists in space around a magnet or a wire carrying electric current, detected by magnetic force on a test magnet.

k7l19.q: In the iron-filing experiment (Figure 19.2), what does a region with densely packed iron-filing lines indicate?

a.quiz: A stronger magnetic field

k7l19.expl: Where iron filing lines are arranged closely/densely, the magnetic field is stronger; where sparse, it is weaker.

k7l19.q: Outside a bar magnet, what is the direction of magnetic field lines?
opts: From South pole to North pole
From North pole to South pole
Straight up into the sky only

a.quiz: From North pole to South pole

k7l19.expl: Outside a magnet, magnetic field lines go out from the North (N) pole and enter the South (S) pole.

k7l19.q: Do Earth’s magnetic poles coincide with Earth’s geographic North and South poles?
opts: No, Earth’s magnetic poles do not coincide with its geographic poles
Yes, they are at the exact same point

a.quiz: No, Earth’s magnetic poles do not coincide with its geographic poles

k7l19.hint: Check section IV and Figure 19.7 on page 93.
k7l19.expl: Earth’s magnetic poles are offset from and do not coincide with its geographic North and South poles.

k7l19.q: When using a compass to find directions (Figure 19.9), what is the first step with the compass dial?
opts: Keep away from magnets/magnetic materials and align the red north needle tip with the N mark on the dial
Shake the compass violently while walking
Place it directly on a strong bar magnet

a.quiz: Keep away from magnets/magnetic materials and align the red north needle tip with the N mark on the dial

k7l19.expl: Place the compass away from magnets/magnetic objects, hold/set it level, and rotate the dial so the red north tip aligns with N.

k7l19.q: The pattern of iron filings around a magnet is called a magnetic ___.

a.quiz: spectrum

k7l19.sentence: Iron filings form a magnetic spectrum.
k7l19.hint: Formed in Experiment II on page 91.
k7l19.expl: A magnetic spectrum gives a visual picture of the magnetic field around a magnet.

k7l19.q: Outside a magnet, magnetic field lines run from the ___ pole to the South pole.

a.quiz: North

k7l19.hint: Out of N, into S outside the magnet.
k7l19.expl: Outside a bar magnet, magnetic field lines emerge from the North pole and enter the South pole.

k7l19.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k7l19.raw: Outside a magnet, magnetic field lines point from the North pole to the South pole.
k7l19.sentence: Outside a magnet, magnetic field lines point from the North pole to the South pole.
k7l19.expl: This states field-line direction outside a magnet.

k7l19.hint: Three items are compass direction abbreviations in Table 19.1.
k7l19.expl: A scalpel is a lab cutting tool, not a compass direction code.

k7l19.q: In 1820, Oersted showed that a wire carrying electric current produces a magnetic field around it.
k7l19.hint: Check section I and Figure 19.1 on page 90.
k7l19.expl: Closing switch K sends current through wire AB and deflects the magnetic needle, proving a current has a magnetic field.

k7l19.q: Find and correct the mistake: Earth’s magnetic North and South poles are in the exact same spot as Earth’s geographic poles.

a.fix: Earth’s magnetic poles do not coincide with Earth’s geographic poles.

k7l19.raw: Earth’s magnetic poles do not coincide with Earth’s geographic poles.
k7l19.expl: Earth’s magnetic poles are distinct from and do not coincide with its geographic poles.

k7l20.q: What is the role of the soft iron core (lõi sắt non) placed inside the coil of an electromagnet?
opts: To increase the magnetic field of the electromagnet
To turn off the power source automatically

a.quiz: To increase the magnetic field of the electromagnet

k7l20.hint: Check the "EM ĐÃ HỌC" box on page 98.
k7l20.expl: A soft iron core inside the coil strengthens/increases the electromagnet’s magnetic field.

k7l20.q: When is the magnetic field of a simple electromagnet present?
opts: Only while electric current is flowing through the coil
Forever even with no power source and no current
Only when the switch is open and current is zero

a.quiz: Only while electric current is flowing through the coil

k7l20.hint: Electromagnetism here comes from electric current.
k7l20.expl: An electromagnet’s magnetic field exists only while current flows through the coil and changes when current changes.

k7l20.q: In Experiment II (Figure 20.2), what happens to magnetic strength when you increase the number of batteries (cells)?
opts: It attracts more iron paperclips because the magnetic force becomes stronger
The iron nail turns into plastic

a.quiz: It attracts more iron paperclips because the magnetic force becomes stronger

k7l20.hint: More batteries increase current and magnetic pull.
k7l20.expl: Increasing the battery count increases current and strengthens the magnetic force, allowing it to pick up more iron paperclips.

k7l20.q: Why do scrap-yard cranes use electromagnets rather than ordinary permanent magnets to move heavy iron/steel?
opts: Because an electromagnet can be turned on to lift heavy steel and turned off to release it easily
Because permanent magnets cannot lift anything
Because electromagnets are made of paper
Because current is not needed at all

a.quiz: Because an electromagnet can be turned on to lift heavy steel and turned off to release it easily

k7l20.hint: Think about picking up and dropping heavy scrap metal at the right place.
k7l20.expl: An electromagnet’s magnetism can be switched on/off and controlled by current, making lifting and dropping heavy steel/iron easy.

k7l20.q: In the electric bell diagram (Figure 20.4), what happens when button E is pressed?
opts: Current flows into electromagnet A, attracting striker C to hit gong D
Gong D flies away into space

a.quiz: Current flows into electromagnet A, attracting striker C to hit gong D

k7l20.hint: Follow the steps in section II.2 on page 98.
k7l20.expl: Pressing E sends current through electromagnet A, which attracts striker C to strike bell D and repeat the ringing cycle.

k7l20.q: Placing a soft ___ core inside the coil increases the magnetic field of the electromagnet.

a.quiz: iron

k7l20.sentence: A soft iron core strengthens the electromagnet.
k7l20.hint: It is a magnetic metal core inside the coil.
k7l20.expl: A soft iron core inside the coil makes the electromagnet’s magnetic field stronger.

k7l20.q: In Figure 20.2, copper wire is wound around a plastic tube with an ___ nail inside.

a.quiz: iron

k7l20.expl: Winding copper wire around a tube with an iron nail inside forms a simple electromagnet when connected to a battery.

k7l20.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k7l20.raw: A soft iron core inside the coil increases the magnetic field of the electromagnet.
k7l20.sentence: A soft iron core inside the coil increases the magnetic field of the electromagnet.
k7l20.expl: This states the function of the soft iron core.

k7l20.hint: Three items are parts/applications of an electromagnet.
k7l20.expl: A barometer is for atmospheric pressure, whereas a coil, soft iron core, and electric bell relate to electromagnets.

k7l20.q: Reversing the terminals of the power source in the simple electromagnet circuit changes the magnetic field direction.
k7l20.hint: Check the last test step in section II on page 97.
k7l20.expl: Reversing current direction by swapping battery terminals reverses the magnetic field direction.

k7l20.q: Find and correct the mistake: An electromagnet keeps its magnetic field permanently after you open the switch and cut off all current.

a.fix: An electromagnet’s magnetic field exists only while current flows through the coil and disappears when current stops.

k7l20.raw: An electromagnet’s magnetic field exists only while current flows through the coil and disappears when current stops.
k7l20.hint: What happens when you open the switch in Figure 20.2?
k7l20.expl: Unlike a permanent magnet, an electromagnet’s magnetic field depends on electric current and exists only while current flows.

k7l21.q: What happens if metabolism stops completely in a living organism?
opts: The organism grows twice as fast
The organism dies because metabolism is required for survival
The organism turns into a rock

a.quiz: The organism dies because metabolism is required for survival

k7l21.hint: All living organisms continuously exchange matter and energy.
k7l21.expl: Every living body constantly exchanges matter and energy with its environment; if metabolism stops, the organism dies.

k7l21.q: Which energy conversion occurs when a person runs fast?
opts: Light energy turns into sound energy only
Chemical energy from food is transformed into mechanical energy (movement) and thermal energy (heat)

a.quiz: Chemical energy from food is transformed into mechanical energy (movement) and thermal energy (heat)

k7l21.hint: Think about why your body moves and warms up when running.
k7l21.expl: During running, chemical energy is converted into mechanical energy for muscle movement and thermal energy that warms the body.

k7l21.q: How are metabolism and energy transformation related?
opts: They are completely unrelated and never happen together
They are always closely linked and occur together
Metabolism happens only in rocks; energy transformation happens only in stars

a.quiz: They are always closely linked and occur together

k7l21.hint: Check the summary statement at the end of section I.
k7l21.expl: Metabolism and energy transformation are inseparable: transforming substances involves transforming energy.

k7l21.q: Why do breathing rate, heart rate, sweating, and thirst increase during heavy exercise?
opts: Because the body stops all metabolism
Because cells need more oxygen and nutrients for energy, releasing heat and losing water through sweat

a.quiz: Because cells need more oxygen and nutrients for energy, releasing heat and losing water through sweat

k7l21.hint: Check the opening question and "EM CÓ THỂ" box on pages 99–100.
k7l21.expl: Intense activity increases energy demand, raising heart/breathing rates, releasing thermal energy (sweating), and causing thirst.

k7l21.q: Which life processes depend on metabolism and energy transformation (Figures 21.1 & 21.2)?
opts: Survival, growth, development, sensitivity, movement, and reproduction

a.quiz: Survival, growth, development, sensitivity, movement, and reproduction

k7l21.hint: Look at the potato plant and chicken life cycles in Figures 21.1 and 21.2.
k7l21.expl: Synthesized organic matter builds cells for growth, development, and reproduction, while released energy powers movement and responses.

k7l21.q: ___ is the conversion of energy from one form into another, such as light energy into chemical energy.

a.quiz: Energy transformation

k7l21.sentence: Energy transformation converts energy between forms.
k7l21.hint: Quang năng thành hóa năng; hóa năng thành cơ năng, nhiệt năng.
k7l21.expl: Energy transformation converts energy between forms to support life processes.

k7l21.q: When metabolism stops in a living organism, the organism will ___.

a.quiz: die

k7l21.expl: Continuous metabolism is required for survival; when it stops, the organism dies.

k7l21.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k7l21.raw: Metabolism and energy transformation help organisms survive, grow, develop, move, and reproduce.
k7l21.sentence: Metabolism and energy transformation help organisms survive, grow, develop, move, and reproduce.
k7l21.expl: This summarizes the roles of metabolism and energy transformation.

k7l21.hint: Three items are forms of energy mentioned in section I.
k7l21.expl: Distilled water is a substance, whereas light energy, chemical energy, and thermal energy are forms of energy.

k7l21.q: Organic substances synthesized during metabolism provide building materials for cells, growth, and reproduction.
k7l21.expl: Synthesized organic molecules serve as raw materials to construct new cells and tissues for growth and reproduction.

k7l21.q: Find and correct the mistake: Metabolism takes in wastes from the environment and releases nutrients that the organism needs to survive.

a.fix: Metabolism takes in needed substances from the environment, transforms them for the body, and releases waste substances.

k7l21.raw: Metabolism takes in needed substances from the environment, transforms them for the body, and releases waste substances.
k7l21.hint: Swap needed substances and waste substances.
k7l21.expl: Organisms absorb useful substances/nutrients and eliminate waste substances back into the environment.

k7l22.q: What are the raw materials (inputs) and products (outputs) of photosynthesis?
opts: Inputs: glucose and oxygen; Outputs: water and carbon dioxide
Inputs: water and carbon dioxide; Outputs: glucose (organic matter) and oxygen
Inputs: salt and iron; Outputs: nitrogen and helium
Inputs: starch and light; Outputs: soil and clay

a.quiz: Inputs: water and carbon dioxide; Outputs: glucose (organic matter) and oxygen

k7l22.hint: Check the word equation for photosynthesis on page 101.
k7l22.expl: Plants take in water (H2O) and carbon dioxide (CO2) and use light energy and chlorophyll to produce glucose (C6H12O6) and oxygen (O2).

k7l22.q: What energy transformation occurs during photosynthesis?
opts: Chemical energy turns into light energy
Light energy (quang năng) is converted into chemical energy (hóa năng) stored in organic compounds
Electrical energy turns into mechanical energy

a.quiz: Light energy (quang năng) is converted into chemical energy (hóa năng) stored in organic compounds

k7l22.hint: Sunlight energy is stored in glucose and starch.
k7l22.expl: Photosynthesis transforms solar light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose and starch.

k7l22.q: What is the main function of stomata (khí khổng) in photosynthesis?
opts: To absorb minerals from deep soil
To let carbon dioxide enter the leaf and oxygen exit to the environment
To anchor the tree trunk in wind
To turn water into solid ice

a.quiz: To let carbon dioxide enter the leaf and oxygen exit to the environment

k7l29.hint: Check section II and Figure 29.2 on page 123.

k7l29.q: What happens to grape leaves lacking nitrogen (N) and tomato leaves lacking magnesium (Mg) in Figure 29.5?
opts: Grape leaves turn yellow (lack of N); tomato leaves turn yellow and curled (lack of Mg)
Both turn into bright blue flowers

a.quiz: Grape leaves turn yellow (lack of N); tomato leaves turn yellow and curled (lack of Mg)

k7l29.expl: Nitrogen deficiency causes yellowing leaves (needed for chlorophyll/protein), and magnesium deficiency causes yellowing and curling in tomato leaves.

k7l29.q: How do Rhizobium bacteria living in root nodules of legume plants (cây họ Đậu, Figure 29.7) help plants?
opts: They convert atmospheric nitrogen gas into usable nitrogen compounds for the plant and enrich the soil
They eat all the roots of the plant
They block water from entering the stem

a.quiz: They convert atmospheric nitrogen gas into usable nitrogen compounds for the plant and enrich the soil

k7l29.hint: Check the "Em có biết?" box on page 126.
k7l29.expl: Rhizobium bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen into absorbable forms, supplying nitrogen to legumes and enriching soil fertility.

k7l29.q: Which nutrients do animals need in large quantities versus small quantities?
opts: Large quantities: proteins, carbohydrates, lipids; Small quantities: vitamins and minerals
Large quantities: vitamins only; Small quantities: water and protein
Large quantities: soil minerals only; Small quantities: oxygen
Animals need no nutrients at all

a.quiz: Large quantities: proteins, carbohydrates, lipids; Small quantities: vitamins and minerals

k7l29.expl: Animals require macronutrients (proteins, carbohydrates, lipids) in large amounts and micronutrients (vitamins and minerals) in small amounts.

k7l29.q: Due to its ___, water molecules attract each other and dissolve many substances.

a.quiz: polarity

k7l29.sentence: Water’s polarity makes it a good solvent.
k7l29.hint: The oxygen end is slightly negative and hydrogen ends are slightly positive.
k7l29.expl: Water’s polarity makes it a versatile biological solvent.

k7l29.q: ___ bacteria in root nodules of legume plants convert air nitrogen into usable nitrogen for crops.

a.quiz: Rhizobium

k7l29.expl: Rhizobium bacteria fix nitrogen gas into forms plants can absorb.

k7l29.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k7l29.raw: Water builds cells, dissolves and transports nutrients, participates in metabolism, and regulates temperature.
k7l29.sentence: Water builds cells, dissolves and transports nutrients, participates in metabolism, and regulates temperature.
k7l29.expl: This summarizes the main roles of water in living things.

k7l29.hint: Three items are nutrients animals need in large amounts.
k7l29.expl: Vitamins are required in small amounts, whereas proteins, carbohydrates, and lipids are needed in large amounts.

k7l29.q: If a person loses water due to vomiting, high fever, or diarrhea, they should rehydrate promptly with water or oral rehydration solution.
k7l29.expl: Severe water loss disrupts vital body processes, so lost water and electrolytes must be replenished promptly.

k7l29.q: Find and correct the mistake: In a water molecule, the oxygen end is positively charged and the hydrogen ends are negatively charged.

a.fix: In a water molecule, the oxygen end is negatively charged and the hydrogen ends are positively charged.

k7l29.raw: In a water molecule, the oxygen end is negatively charged and the hydrogen ends are positively charged.

k7l30.q: What is the pathway of water and dissolved minerals from soil into the plant stem and leaves (Figure 30.1)?
opts: Soil -> root hair cells -> root cortex cells -> root xylem -> stem xylem -> leaves
Leaves -> phloem -> root hair cells -> soil

a.quiz: Soil -> root hair cells -> root cortex cells -> root xylem -> stem xylem -> leaves

k7l30.hint: Follow the arrows in Figure 30.1 on page 127.
k7l30.expl: Water and dissolved minerals enter root hair cells, pass through root cortex cells into root xylem, and rise through stem xylem to leaves.

k7l30.q: How do xylem (mạch gỗ) and phloem (mạch rây) differ in transport direction and substances carried?
opts: Xylem carries water/minerals upward from roots to leaves; phloem carries organic compounds from leaves to storage/using organs
Xylem carries organic food downward; phloem carries water upward
Both carry only air bubbles downward

a.quiz: Xylem carries water/minerals upward from roots to leaves; phloem carries organic compounds from leaves to storage/using organs

k7l30.hint: Check Table 30.1 and Figure 30.2 on page 128.
k7l30.expl: Xylem transports water and minerals upward from roots; phloem transports organic substances made in leaves to other plant organs.

k7l30.q: How does water status control the opening and closing of stomata (Figure 30.3)?
opts: When well watered, guard cells swell and open stomata; when water-deficient, guard cells deflate and close stomata
When water-deficient, stomata open wider forever
Water has no effect on guard cells
Stomata open only when frozen at -10°C

a.quiz: When well watered, guard cells swell and open stomata; when water-deficient, guard cells deflate and close stomata

k7l30.hint: Check section III.1 and Figure 30.3 on page 128.
k7l30.expl: Water uptake makes guard cells turgid and open the pore; water loss makes guard cells flaccid and narrow/close the pore.

k7l30.q: What are the three key roles of transpiration (thoát hơi nước) at the leaves?
opts: Pulling water/minerals up from roots, cooling the leaf, and letting CO2 enter for photosynthesis
Turning leaves into dry wood, stopping photosynthesis, and heating leaves to 80°C
Blocking all minerals at the roots
Pushing water out through the roots into deep rock

a.quiz: Pulling water/minerals up from roots, cooling the leaf, and letting CO2 enter for photosynthesis

k7l30.expl: Transpiration provides the upward pulling force, cools leaf temperature on hot days, and keeps stomata open for CO2 intake.

k7l30.q: Why do gardeners prune some branches and leaves when digging up a tree to transplant it elsewhere?
opts: To reduce leaf surface area and transpiration water loss while damaged roots recover
To make the tree heavier to carry
To stop the roots from ever absorbing water

a.quiz: To reduce leaf surface area and transpiration water loss while damaged roots recover

k7l30.expl: Transplanting damages fine root hairs; trimming some leaves reduces transpiration so the tree does not lose more water than its roots can absorb.

k7l30.q: Water and dissolved minerals travel upward from roots to leaves through ___ vessels.

a.quiz: xylem

k7l30.sentence: Xylem carries water and minerals upward.
k7l30.expl: Xylem conducts water and dissolved minerals upward from roots to stems and leaves.

k7l30.q: Organic substances synthesized in leaves are transported to roots, fruits, and tubers via ___.

a.quiz: phloem

k7l30.hint: The vascular tissue carrying organic food from leaves.
k7l30.expl: Phloem transports organic compounds from leaves to using or storage organs.

k7l30.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k7l30.raw: Root hair cells absorb water and dissolved minerals from soil into the root xylem.
k7l30.sentence: Root hair cells absorb water and dissolved minerals from soil into the root xylem.
k7l30.expl: This describes how plants absorb water and minerals.

odd: Cooling the leaf on hot days
k7l30.hint: Three items are roles of leaf transpiration in section III.2.
k7l30.expl: Turning leaves into solid stone is not a role of transpiration.

k7l30.q: Plants can only absorb soil mineral nutrients when those minerals are dissolved in water.
k7l30.expl: Roots absorb mineral ions only in aqueous solution, so adequate soil moisture is essential for nutrient uptake.

k7l30.q: Find and correct the mistake: Phloem carries water and minerals from roots to leaves, while xylem carries organic food from leaves to roots.

a.fix: Xylem carries water and minerals from roots to leaves, while phloem carries organic substances from leaves to other organs.

k7l30.raw: Xylem carries water and minerals from roots to leaves, while phloem carries organic substances from leaves to other organs.
k7l30.hint: Swap xylem and phloem to match Table 30.1.
k7l30.expl: Xylem conducts water and minerals upward; phloem conducts organic products from leaves.

k7l31.q: What are the three stages of nutrient processing in the human digestive tract (Figure 31.1)?
opts: 1. Ingestion; 2. Digestion into simple nutrients and absorption into blood; 3. Elimination of feces through the anus

a.quiz: 1. Ingestion; 2. Digestion into simple nutrients and absorption into blood; 3. Elimination of feces through the anus

k7l31.hint: Check the three callout boxes in Figure 31.1 on page 131.
k7l31.expl: Food enters the mouth (Stage 1), is digested into simple molecules absorbed into blood (Stage 2), and undigested waste leaves as feces (Stage 3).

k7l31.q: Which part of the human digestive tract absorbs the greatest amount of water?

a.quiz: Large intestine (ruột già)

k7l31.expl: Water is absorbed across digestive organs, with the large intestine (ruột già) absorbing the largest share into the bloodstream.

k7l31.q: According to the 2012 National Institute of Nutrition guideline (40 mL/kg/day), how much water should a 45 kg teenager take in daily?

a.quiz: 1,800 mL (1.8 liters)

k7l31.expl: 45 kg × 40 mL/kg = 1,800 mL (1.8 liters) per day.

k7l31.q: What is the role of the pulmonary circulation (vòng tuần hoàn nhỏ) in humans (Figure 31.5)?
opts: It carries dark-red oxygen-poor blood from the heart to the lungs to pick up O2 and release CO2, returning bright-red blood to the heart
It pumps food directly into the kidneys
It carries bright-red blood from the lungs to the toes without passing the heart
It produces urine in the bladder

a.quiz: It carries dark-red oxygen-poor blood from the heart to the lungs to pick up O2 and release CO2, returning bright-red blood to the heart

k7l31.hint: Follow the upper loop between the heart and lung capillaries in Figure 31.5.
k7l31.expl: Pulmonary circulation sends oxygen-poor blood from the heart to lung capillaries where it gains O2 and releases CO2 before returning to the heart.

k7l31.q: Which consequence can result from consuming too much fat and carbohydrate with insufficient physical activity?
opts: Night blindness from vitamin A deficiency
Excess energy storage leading to obesity, joint strain, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease

a.quiz: Excess energy storage leading to obesity, joint strain, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease

k7l31.expl: Overconsuming fats and carbohydrates creates surplus energy stored as fat, causing obesity and raising risks of joint damage, diabetes, and heart disease.

k7l31.q: Urine is formed by blood filtration in the ___, travels down ureters to the bladder, and exits via the urethra.

a.quiz: kidneys

k7l31.sentence: Kidneys filter blood to produce urine.
k7l31.hint: Shown at the top of Figure 31.4.
k7l31.expl: The kidneys filter wastes and excess water from blood to produce urine.

k7l31.q: In Figure 31.5, ___ circulation carries bright-red oxygen-rich blood and nutrients to nourish body organs.

a.quiz: systemic

k7l31.hint: The larger loop serving body organs (vòng tuần hoàn lớn).
k7l31.expl: Systemic circulation distributes oxygenated blood and nutrients from the heart to all body tissues.

k7l31.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k7l31.raw: Animals take in water through food and drink and eliminate water mainly via urine and sweat.
k7l31.sentence: Animals take in water through food and drink and eliminate water mainly via urine and sweat.
k7l31.expl: This summarizes water intake and loss in animals.

k7l31.hint: Three items are good food hygiene habits in Table 31.1.
k7l31.expl: Eating spoiled food causes food poisoning, whereas eating cooked food, washing hands, and brushing teeth protect health.

k7l31.q: North American kangaroo rats do not need to drink liquid water because they obtain water from the seeds they eat.

k7l31.q: Find and correct the mistake: Pulmonary circulation carries bright-red oxygen-rich blood from the heart to the lungs, where it loses all oxygen.

a.fix: Pulmonary circulation carries dark-red oxygen-poor blood from the heart to the lungs, where it gains oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.

k7l31.raw: Pulmonary circulation carries dark-red oxygen-poor blood from the heart to the lungs, where it gains oxygen and releases carbon dioxide.
k7l31.hint: Check the color and gas exchange in lung capillaries in Figure 31.5.
k7l31.expl: Blood leaving the heart for the lungs is oxygen-poor (dark red) and becomes oxygen-rich (bright red) in the lungs.

k7l32.q: Why must colored water (with red, blue, or purple dye) be used in Experiment 1?
opts: Because pure water is invisible inside plant tissues, whereas dye stains the xylem vessels so water transport is clearly visible
Because dye turns celery into metal
Because plants cannot absorb clear water

The entire stalk turns pitch black
The dye stays only at the bottom outside the stalk

k7l32.q: In Experiment 2 (Figure 32.2), how are Pot A and Pot B prepared differently?
opts: Pot A has all leaves removed, while Pot B keeps all its leaves intact
Pot A is filled with boiling oil; Pot B has ice cubes

Pot A is sealed in metal; Pot B has no bag

k7l32.q: Why must the transparent plastic bag be tied tightly around the plant stem above the soil rather than enclosing the wet soil?

To stop sunlight from reaching the leaves
To keep oxygen out of the room

opts: Transpiration occurs mainly through the leaves of the plant
Roots release water vapor into the sky directly

k7l32.sentence: Colored water shows water transport in stems.

k7l32.expl: Colored water stains the xylem vascular bundles and leaves, making water transport easy to see.

k7l32.q: In Experiment 2, water droplets condense inside the clear plastic bag covering ___ Pot B.

k7l32.q: Arrange the words to make a correct sentence.
k7l32.raw: Colored water rises through xylem vessels in the stem and petioles to stain the leaves.
k7l32.sentence: Colored water rises through xylem vessels in the stem and petioles to stain the leaves.

k7l32.q: Cutting a stained celery stalk crosswise and viewing with a magnifying glass shows dye specifically inside the xylem vascular bundles.
k7l32.expl: Only the xylem conducting strands become stained, confirming that xylem transports water upward.

k7l32.q: Find and correct the mistake: In Experiment 2, the bag over leafless Pot A fills with water droplets while leafy Pot B stays completely dry.
